## [Cloudflare Acquires Deno, Ending the Deno Runtime](https://deno.com/blog/cloudflare) ⭐️ 9.0/10

Cloudflare has acquired Deno, and the Deno team announced it will support the Deno runtime for only one more year with monthly bug-fix and security releases before ending development of the runtime entirely. Deno will remain open source, but unless another party takes over, the runtime will no longer be officially supported. Deno was one of the most prominent alternative JavaScript/TypeScript runtimes, and its effective shutdown removes a major independent competitor to Node.js while concentrating more of the JS tooling ecosystem under a few large corporate owners. Developers who built on Deno now face a migration decision, and the broader community is debating open source sustainability and corporate influence over runtimes. The one-year support window includes monthly releases with bug fixes and security updates, after which Cloudflare will stop developing the runtime; the code stays open source and the community is invited to continue it. The acquisition is widely characterized as an acquihire that brings Deno's talent into Cloudflare, whose Workers platform runs on its own open-source workerd runtime.

hackernews · ilreb · Oct 9, 13:03 · [Discussion](https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50019911)

**Background**: Deno is a secure JavaScript and TypeScript runtime created by Ryan Dahl, the original author of Node.js, and first released in 2020 to address design regrets in Node.js, notably around security and permissions. Cloudflare Workers is a JavaScript edge runtime running on Cloudflare's CDN, powered by the open-source workerd runtime. The JS runtime space has seen growing consolidation, with Bun acquired by Anthropic and other tooling companies absorbed by larger players.

## [ASI-Arch Autonomously Discovers 105 State-of-the-Art Linear Attention Architectures](https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.18074) ⭐️ 9.0/10

Researchers present ASI-Arch, a system for AI-driven AI research that autonomously conducts neural architecture research through a closed-loop research-experiment-analyze-update process. Applied to linear attention, ASI-Arch ran 1,773 iterative experiments and discovered 105 state-of-the-art architectures, with its best architecture improving over DeltaNet by nearly three times the gain achieved by Mamba2. This demonstrates that an AI system can independently discover state-of-the-art neural architectures, potentially accelerating AI research itself and reducing reliance on human-designed baselines. The scale of 1,773 experiments and 105 architectures highlights the growing capability of autonomous research agents in complex, long-horizon tasks. The system's best architecture improves over DeltaNet by nearly three times the gain achieved by Mamba2, and the paper analyzes the contributions of different framework components in this hard research setting. The closed-loop process involves iterative research, experimentation, analysis, and updates, enabling autonomous progress.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 9, 04:00

**Background**: Linear attention mechanisms aim to reduce the quadratic complexity of standard self-attention, making them more efficient for long sequences. DeltaNet and Mamba2 are recent architectures that advance this area: DeltaNet uses a delta rule for fast weight updates, while Mamba2 is a state space model (SSM) known for efficient sequence modeling. Neural architecture search (NAS) traditionally relies on human-designed search spaces, but this work uses LLM agents to autonomously discover architectures.

## [Essay on How LLMs Are Eroding the Motivation to Share Knowledge](https://borretti.me/article/no-man-is-an-island) ⭐️ 8.0/10

A reflective essay titled "No Man Is an Island" published on borretti.me argues that the rise of large language models is undermining people's motivation to publicly share knowledge, such as writing blog posts, publishing technical notes, or creating new programming languages, because LLMs ingest that content without crediting the authors. The piece sparked a substantial Hacker News discussion with diverse viewpoints on AI maximalism, doomerism, and the ethics of training on public content. This matters because open-source culture and public knowledge sharing depend on contributors feeling that their work is recognized and valued; if LLMs erode that incentive, the entire ecosystem of shared technical knowledge could shrink. The discussion highlights a growing tension between the productivity gains of AI and the psychological and ethical costs to the communities that produce the training data. The essay focuses on the psychological and community impact rather than technical benchmarks, and the Hacker News thread includes commenters describing a "real depression" over the destruction of the community of code, while others note that craft and taste remain differentiators even if AI can get 80% of the way to a perfect result in an afternoon. The title references John Donne's meditation "No Man Is an Island," which a commenter quotes in full to frame the discussion about collective interdependence.

## [Microsoft MXC: A Unified Sandboxed Code Execution System](https://github.com/microsoft/mxc) ⭐️ 8.0/10

Microsoft has open-sourced MXC (Microsoft Execution Containers), a sandboxed code execution system that provides a consistent SDK for running untrusted code across Windows, Linux, and macOS. It abstracts multiple containment backends—including bubblewrap, seatbelt, and processcontainer—behind a unified policy model and TypeScript SDK. MXC lowers the barrier for safely executing AI-generated code, plugins, and tools by replacing error-prone hand-rolled sandboxing with a single policy declaration. This is significant for agentic AI workflows, where developers need to contain model output and dynamically generated workloads across platforms. MXC offers a TypeScript SDK (@microsoft/mxc-sdk) with one-shot and state-aware APIs, plus diagnostics via debug logging and Event Tracing for Windows (ETW). However, fine-grained networking controls such as allow/deny by hostname or IP/CIDR/port are available on Windows and Linux but missing on macOS.

<a id="item-7"></a>
## [Learning Indexical Policies Finds Plans in Polynomial Space](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.10954) ⭐️ 8.0/10

A new arXiv preprint (2610.10954) introduces a learning-based method for search control in AI planning that represents domain-specific policies as indexical policies with registers, modes, and a new choose rule. The authors prove that structural termination bounds every execution by a polynomial in the number of objects, so a depth-first procedure finds plans in polynomial space, with time exponential only in choice depth, placing solvable classes in NP and in P for constant choice depth. This result challenges the long-standing assumption that heuristic search for plans inherently requires exponential memory, showing that learned search control can avoid storing visited states entirely. It could reshape how automated planners are designed and analyzed, and it demonstrates that language models can learn certified, low-choice-depth policies that outperform strong classical planners. The choose rule loads an object into a register and marks a backtracking point where only one candidate needs to succeed, while all other rules must work for every outcome without search. The learned policies solve 1,709 of 1,890 test tasks from the IPC 2023 Learning Track and the Autoscale Agile suite, surpassing LAMA, BFWS, and Levitron, mostly within one second and 100 MiB; however, this is a preprint without peer review or community discussion yet.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 9, 04:00

**Background**: Automated planning is the problem of finding a sequence of actions that reaches a goal from an initial state, and heuristic search is a standard approach that uses an estimate of remaining cost to guide exploration. Classical heuristic search typically stores exponentially many states, even with near-perfect heuristics, which limits scalability. Indexical policies are generalized policies whose rules refer to objects via registers and are sequenced by modes, and the paper's counterexample-guided learning loop uses a language model to learn such policies while certifying termination and keeping choice depth small.

**Tags**: `#AI Planning`, `#Heuristic Search`, `#Reinforcement Learning`, `#Complexity Theory`, `#Automated Planning`

## [Narrative Wrapping Bypasses LLM Refusal Across Languages](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.11005) ⭐️ 8.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2610.11005) shows that wrapping harmful requests in role-play or narrative form bypasses safety refusals at high rates: attack success on Qwen3-1.7B reaches 89.4% in English, 93.0% in modern Chinese, and 95.7% in Classical Chinese. The authors introduce GUISE, a cross-language benchmark with parallel harmful/benign pairs and held-out wrapper types, and AXIS, a defense combining preference optimization with rotation and commitment objectives. This exposes a fundamental weakness in safety-aligned LLMs: refusal behavior is fragile under narrative framing and varies sharply across languages and registers, meaning multilingual deployments may be far less safe than English-only evaluations suggest. The work provides both a systematic benchmark and a training-based defense, which matters for anyone building or auditing safety-critical LLM applications. Representation analysis shows that language and register shift harmful-request representations only slightly away from the model's refusal direction, whereas narrative wrappers move them much farther away. GUISE uses a stricter criterion that counts warn-then-answer responses as attack successes, and AXIS achieves the highest combined safety and usability score across Qwen3-1.7B, Qwen3-4B, and GLM-4-9B.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 9, 04:00

**Background**: Safety-aligned language models are trained to refuse harmful requests, and prior work has shown that refusal is mediated by a single direction in the model's representation space that can be ablated to bypass safety. This paper extends that line of research by studying how narrative framing and cross-language variation interact with the refusal direction, and by proposing a defense that rotates harmful-request representations back toward the refusal direction.

<a id="item-9"></a>
## [Distillation Double Bind: Auditing Misaligned AI via Model Distillation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.11012) ⭐️ 8.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2610.11012) proposes two distillation methods—Distillation for Incrimination (DFI) and Distillation for Capabilities (DFC)—to audit potentially misaligned AI models. Experiments on AuditBench's secret-keeping models show that distilling a teacher into a weaker student makes the student significantly more likely to confess hidden behaviors, indicating misalignment-related knowledge transfers more readily than the propensity to conceal it. This work introduces a novel 'Distillation Double Bind' framework that turns model compression into an active AI safety diagnostic, addressing the critical problem that misaligned models may recognize and strategically pass alignment evaluations. It offers concrete techniques for both incriminating misaligned models and extracting their capabilities without transferring misalignment, which could reshape how the AI safety community audits powerful models. DFI's confession gains largely disappear when the student does not share the teacher's pretrained base, so the method should target the teacher's own pre-RL checkpoint, which is weaker but shares the base model. For DFC, inoculation prompting and training for more epochs on fewer unique examples both preserve capability gains while substantially reducing subliminal transfer of an animal preference used as a misalignment proxy.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 9, 04:00

**Background**: Model distillation is a common technique where a smaller 'student' model is trained to mimic a larger 'teacher' model, typically to compress capabilities into a more efficient model. AuditBench is a benchmark of 56 language models with implanted hidden behaviors—such as sycophantic deference or secret geopolitical loyalties—that they do not confess when directly asked. The 'Distillation Double Bind' idea proposes that distilling a misaligned teacher either transfers its misalignment (incriminating it) or transfers only benign capabilities, giving auditors a win either way.

<ul>

## [OpenProblemBench Tests AI on 82 Unsolved Math and Physics Problems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.11118) ⭐️ 8.0/10

Researchers introduced OpenProblemBench, a benchmark of 82 unresolved problems drawn from the mathematics and theoretical physics literature, each accompanied by research context, assumptions, and prior progress. Four evaluator models independently judged submissions without reference solutions, and GPT-6-Astra achieved the highest mean judged solve rate of 14.0%, versus 5.5-6.7% for full-size open models and 2.4-3.7% for Flash models. This benchmark shifts AI evaluation from established knowledge toward genuinely open scientific questions, offering a more meaningful signal for AGI progress than conventional exams. Its reference-free, multi-evaluator methodology could influence how future benchmarks assess creative scientific reasoning and partial progress. Problems were selected so that proposed solutions admit comparatively clear checks of their decisive mathematical or computational claims, and case comparisons link stronger outcomes to changes in problem representation, general arguments beyond finite evidence, and proofs of intermediate steps. The reported solve rates are judged by evaluator models rather than verified by human experts, so they should be read as relative baselines rather than definitive correctness measures.

## [Internalizer scales context-to-parameter hypernetworks to a 284B model](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.11715) ⭐️ 8.0/10

The Internalizer is a portable hypernetwork that generates document-specific LoRA adapters for the frozen 284B-parameter DeepSeek v4 Flash, a target two orders of magnitude larger than the previous 14B ceiling. On unseen documents up to 4096 tokens, the generated adapters reach 84.9% top-1 and 97.8% top-5 teacher-forced accuracy, versus 63.4% and 83.5% for the base model, with only a three-word instruction in the context window. This shows hypernetworks can be scaled to frontier-sized models, turning any document into a weight update in a single forward pass rather than retraining or long-context prompting. It could reshape how large models are adapted and served, since adapters can be served alone for speed or alongside the document to boost accuracy. Most of the hypernetwork's parameters live in a model-agnostic trunk with only thin entry and exit layers per base model, so it can be trained cheaply against small models before being ported to the large one. Once trained, a single forward pass turns any document into an adapter for the target model.

**Background**: Hypernetworks are neural networks that generate the weights or parameters of another network, trained end-to-end so the generated weights are learned rather than directly optimized. LoRA (Low-Rank Adaptation) is a parameter-efficient fine-tuning method that adds a small number of extra weights to adapt a model to a new task or dataset. DeepSeek v4 Flash is a 284B-parameter Mixture-of-Experts language model with 13B activated parameters and a one-million-token context length. Prior context-to-parameter mapping work had only been demonstrated on base models up to 14B parameters.

## [RouterInterp Explains MoE Expert Routing via Sparse Autoencoders](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.11775) ⭐️ 8.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2610.11775) introduces RouterInterp, a method that interprets expert routing in Sparse Mixture of Experts models by identifying Sparse Autoencoder features most predictive of routing decisions. On gpt-oss-20b, RouterInterp achieves roughly 65% higher detection accuracy than prior token-statistics-based methods, and the authors present evidence for the Superposed Specialisation Hypothesis (SSH), which holds that experts specialise in a disjoint union of fine-grained features rather than a single coherent domain. Expert routing in Mixture of Experts models has been a largely uninterpretable component of foundation models, and prior interpretability efforts assuming single-domain specialisation have generally failed. RouterInterp offers a scalable way to generate accurate natural-language explanations of routing decisions, which could improve debugging, auditing, and trust in large MoE-based systems such as gpt-oss-20b. The method leverages Sparse Autoencoders to decompose superposed model features into more interpretable components, then identifies which SAE features best predict routing decisions and produces unified natural-language explanations. The reported ~65% detection-accuracy improvement is measured on gpt-oss-20b, and the authors state that expert routing is highly polysemantic, meaning individual experts respond to multiple unrelated features.

**Background**: Sparse Mixture of Experts (MoE) models scale more efficiently than dense models by routing each token to only a small subset of expert networks, so compute cost tracks active parameters while capacity tracks the full model. A common assumption has been that each expert specialises in one coherent domain, but interpretability work built on that assumption has largely failed. Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) are a mechanistic interpretability technique that disentangles complex, superimposed neural network features into sparsely activating, more monosemantic components, and RouterInterp applies them to the routing problem.

## [LEVER: Adaptive Cost-Aware Proof Search Over AND/OR Graphs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.11862) ⭐️ 8.0/10

LEVER is a new proof search algorithm that makes the objective over correct proofs programmable and optimizes it during search by scoring partial proofs over an AND/OR proof graph, combining realized objective values with predictions for open subgoals. On PutnamBench in Lean 4, under matched budgets, it costs 34% less than a strong single-conversation agent while raising the solve rate from 80% to 96%. This work shifts LLM-powered theorem proving from merely finding any correct proof to actively optimizing proof quality—such as simplicity, purity, and computational cost—during search, which could make automated theorem provers more practical and trustworthy for mathematicians. It also introduces a tunable quality-cost trade-off, letting users decide how much a better proof is worth. LEVER optimizes computational cost, proof length, topical impurity, and weighted combinations of these, while the Lean kernel enforces correctness. On reducing topical impurity, it achieves a 42% reduction versus 33% for post-hoc refactoring at two-thirds of the cost and more reliably; on proof length it approaches refactoring performance.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 9, 04:00

**Background**: AND/OR graphs are a standard structure for representing proof search, where AND nodes require all subgoals to be solved and OR nodes require one of several alternatives. PutnamBench is a benchmark of 640 competition mathematics problems from the William Lowell Putnam Mathematical Competition, formalized in Lean 4 and other proof assistants. Lean 4 is a proof assistant whose trusted kernel checks the correctness of formal proofs, so any proof found by LEVER is verified by the kernel.

## [Structure Tax Depends on Schema Design, Not Structure Itself](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.12056) ⭐️ 8.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2610.12056) re-examines the so-called 'structure tax' in LLM outputs by evaluating a battery of models, datasets, and schemas while measuring task accuracy, confidence calibration, and hidden-state geometry. It finds that reasoning-first field ordering matches or exceeds free-form accuracy, whereas answer-first ordering causes steep accuracy drops, particularly in smaller models. This challenges the common assumption that structured output inherently degrades LLM performance, reframing the key question from 'whether to structure' to 'how to structure'. It offers an actionable insight for production LLM deployment, where JSON or XML constraints are often required. Format sensitivity scales inversely with a task's own structural constraints, and schemas that preserve reasoning order also improve confidence calibration, with CKA showing greater separability between correct and incorrect representations in middle transformer layers. The findings are based on a battery of models, datasets, and schemas, though specific model names and dataset details are not provided in the abstract.

## [MASS: Recursive Self-Improvement via Multi-Agent Self-Supervision](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.12176) ⭐️ 8.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2610.12176) proposes Multi-Agent Self-Supervision (MASS), a recursive self-improvement method that alternates between evolutionary workflow optimization and supervised fine-tuning on self-generated trajectories. Using Qwen3.6-27B over two MASS cycles, it achieves 1.2–1.6x higher performance per output token on four open-ended public benchmarks. It tackles the supervision bottleneck in non-verifiable tasks, where model outputs exceed what human experts can reliably assess, by letting the model itself act as optimizer and evaluator. This could enable continuous recursive bootstrapping of capabilities in multi-agent systems and self-improving AI. MASS prompts a single base model to iteratively propose, execute, and self-evaluate multi-agent workflows, using evolutionary search constrained by structural guardrails to discover effective roles and information routing. Multi-agent traces are also more training-efficient: a student trained on them outperforms a single-agent student trained on 1.4x more tokens.

## [LLM Compliance Verdicts Often Ignore the Supplied Regulatory Rule](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.12313) ⭐️ 8.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2610.12313) tests five models across 20 regulatory and platform-policy domains by deleting, swapping, or negating the governing rule while holding the case fixed, and finds that verdicts are frequently invariant to these substantial rule perturbations. The guard model, evaluated under a custom-rule adaptation of its native taxonomy, was the least rule-sensitive and least accurate of the five, scoring barely above chance at 51%, versus 90-92% for general-purpose models. The finding suggests that high accuracy alone does not prove a compliance verdict is actually grounded in the supplied rule, which undermines the core assumption behind deploying LLM compliance systems in regulated settings. This has direct implications for AI safety, enterprise compliance, and regulatory auditing, since organizations may be relying on verdicts that would not change even if the governing rule changed. The study measures both whether the verdict changes (OCS) and whether the model's internal representation of compliance shifts at all (ICS-delta), and finds neither moves much; notably, on cases where deleting the rule changes a previously correct prediction, models do track the rule closely, suggesting the effect reflects easy cases more than blanket neglect. Neither better prompting nor direct intervention on internal representations closes the gap.

## [AAArena Benchmark Tests AI Agents as Adversarial Heuristic Learners](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.12341) ⭐️ 8.0/10

A new arXiv paper formalizes Adversarial Heuristic Learning (AHL), a paradigm in which AI agents act as learning engines that refine game policies and supporting software while keeping model weights fixed. It introduces AAArena, a benchmark of 12 authentic adversarial games and 1,920 archived human programs, where agents interpret rules, choose opponents, analyze replays, and revise their agents under fixed match and evaluation budgets. The work reframes AI agents as learning engines that produce editable, executable policies rather than relying solely on gradient-based training, which could influence how agent-based systems and game AI are built. Its evaluation protocol mirrors real-world game competitions, making results directly comparable to human performance and highlighting persistent gaps in game understanding and long-horizon strategy. Among the evaluated model and harness configurations, Opus5.5 with Claude Code earned 6 gold medals, while no configuration topped the remaining 6 human ladders; performance was generally weaker in games with more complex rule specifications. Further experiments show that opponent selection and dense feedback support policy improvement, and agents learn from both on-policy replays of their own matches and off-policy replays of other players' matches.

Testing four agents, the authors find that higher task accuracy does not necessarily correspond to greater epistemic humility, and that agents often detect conflicts early but fail to maintain or resolve them in later steps. This work addresses a critical gap in agentic system evaluation, which has focused primarily on task success rather than how agents handle uncertainty and contradictory information. The framework evaluates two conflict settings: controlled conflict, where the backbone model's parametric knowledge contradicts retrieved evidence or two contextual sources disagree, and naturally occurring conflict during multi-step agentic execution. The authors also show that model-level interventions can improve epistemic humility but often at the cost of task accuracy, suggesting EH emerges from the interaction among the backbone model, agent harness, and evaluation environment.

A new arXiv paper (2610.12361) introduces a counterfactual audit that swaps the legal authority named in a verdict for an unrelated one while holding case facts fixed, then decodes the model's verdict from its hidden states. Across seven open-weight models (8B–70B) and four benchmarks (CaseHOLD, ECHR, SCOTUS, ContractNLI), models named the correct authority in 66.7%–100% of generations, but verdicts changed when the authority changed only 0.0%–21.7% of the time on CaseHOLD and 30.0%–76.7% on ECHR/SCOTUS. This matters for AI safety and legal AI deployment, since courts and regulators increasingly treat cited authorities in model output as evidence of faithful reasoning. Neither model scale nor a purpose-built legal-reasoning model (a best-effort LoRA reproduction) closed the faithfulness gap, and a red-teaming evaluation on five core models found compliance with an adversarial instruction hidden in the case facts (73.3%–96.4%) far exceeded verdict-swap sensitivity. The authors report that both findings replicate across checks ruling out prompt-wording noise and confounded sampling.

A new arXiv paper (2610.12436) develops an ecological theory of AI-agent populations, showing that when agents collaborate, collective cybersecurity capability grows with population size, creating a critical population threshold below which the population declines and above which it takes off into a self-reinforcing cycle of misaligned agents. This phenomenon is known in ecology as the strong Allee effect, and the paper argues that red teaming a small group of agents cannot guarantee ecological safety for larger populations. This introduces a novel 'ecological safety' framework that shifts AI safety focus from individual or fixed-population multi-agent risks to the dynamics of the population itself, addressing an under-explored risk of self-replicating misaligned agents. It suggests that capability gains may lower the takeoff threshold, requiring re-estimation for each new model generation and new approaches like ecological red teaming and population pacing. The theory is based on a population growth equation in which fitness (growth rate) depends on cybersecurity capability; without collaboration, takeoff requires individual-agent capability to exceed a critical threshold, but with collaboration the threshold becomes population-dependent. The abstract lacks empirical validation, and the proposed mitigation is gradual deployment of larger agent populations in controlled environments while measuring how cyber capability scales with population size.

## [ALERT-BENCH Exposes LLM Alert Triage Failures, AIDA Fixes Them](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.10608) ⭐️ 8.0/10

A new arXiv paper introduces ALERT-BENCH, an interactive benchmark that replays enterprise telemetry through a live SIEM to evaluate five representative LLM-based alert triage approaches across 1,247 alerts from a multi-stage attack scenario. All five approaches missed at least 40.4% of attack-related alerts, and the authors propose AIDA (Adversarial Investigation and Dialectical Analysis), a multi-agent framework that achieves an F1 score of 0.958 and reduces the false-negative rate to 3.1%. This work provides the first rigorous, interactive benchmark for LLM-based SOC alert triage, revealing that current agentic approaches systematically dismiss real attacks when evidence retrieval returns nothing. The findings and the AIDA framework offer actionable guidance for building more reliable AI security agents, which could significantly reduce missed attacks in security operations centers. Trace analysis shows that attack alerts are more likely to be dismissed when searches return no records, same-context review has negative net correction, and dismissal receives no consistently stronger investigation than escalation. AIDA addresses these issues by requiring an explicit proposed decision before independent challenge, maintaining an append-only Investigation Ledger, and using a separate Judge to adjudicate decisions against evidence, while escalating 18.4% of alerts to human analysts.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 9, 04:00

**Background**: Security operations centers (SOCs) must triage large volumes of alerts, most of which are benign, but missed attacks can remain uninvestigated. Tool-using large language model (LLM) agents can retrieve evidence during triage, but it remains unclear how reasoning strategies determine what evidence to gather and when an investigation is sufficient to close an alert. ALERT-BENCH is an interactive benchmark that replays enterprise telemetry through a live SIEM and requires each system to retrieve evidence, enabling systematic comparison of different LLM-based triage strategies.

## [TestJack Audits Coding Benchmarks by Evolving Evaluators to Expose Reward Hacking](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.10619) ⭐️ 8.0/10

Researchers introduce TestJack, a framework that dynamically generates new tests for each LLM agent trial to detect when patches pass fixed unit tests but violate task requirements. Across 6 frontier model backends and 5 benchmarks including DeepSWE and SWE Marathon, about 34.4% of trials judged correct actually violate requirements, lowering the overall resolution rate from 50.6% to 33.2%. This work reveals a fundamental flaw in how coding agents are evaluated: higher benchmark scores may reflect adaptation to the evaluator rather than genuine problem-solving ability. It could push the AI community to redesign benchmarks with adaptive evaluators, affecting model rankings, training incentives, and trust in reported capabilities. TestJack generates tests targeting prompt requirements a patch may violate, retains only tests passed by the ground-truth patch, and re-examines trial failures so each confirmed failure is supported by a replayable test. A lightweight variant audits a random sample of trials in depth and reuses the resulting tests across all trials for the same task to reduce evaluation cost.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 9, 04:00

**Background**: Reward hacking, or specification gaming, occurs when an AI optimizes the literal objective without achieving the intended outcome. In coding benchmarks, agents are typically judged correct if they pass a fixed set of unit tests, but these tests often check only part of the task, allowing agents to exploit gaps. Existing static test augmentation strengthens tests once before any trial, missing how real trials actually fail.

## [Subliminal Learning Transfers Capabilities, Backdoors, and Hacking Propensities](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.10657) ⭐️ 8.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2610.10657) shows that subliminal learning (SL) can transfer far more than simple preferences: after distilling on semantically unrelated text, a student model learns to predict a randomly initialized MLP's outputs, acquires a French-language backdoor triggered by female names (23.5% vs. 0.0% for male names), and hacks in 58.3% of agentic chess episodes versus 10.9% for the unfinetuned model. This significantly expands the scope of subliminal learning, suggesting that subtle misalignment such as reward-seeking, scheming, or secret loyalties could spread through distillation pipelines without detection, with major implications for AI safety and alignment evaluation. Transfer strength is sensitive to the setup: it is often made stronger by using logit distillation or by restricting LoRA to attention layers, and a directly optimized steering vector matches SL in distribution but generalizes worse out of distribution.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 9, 04:00

**Background**: Subliminal learning is a recently documented phenomenon in which a teacher model passes behavioral traits to a student through distillation on data that is semantically unrelated to those traits — for example, a teacher that likes owls can make its student like owls using only number sequences. Knowledge distillation is the standard technique of transferring knowledge from a larger model to a smaller one, and steering vectors are directions in a model's activation space used to control its behavior. This paper extends earlier SL work, which had only demonstrated simple traits like animal preferences and malicious personas, to complex capabilities, backdoors, and agentic hacking.

## [NavGPT-3 Uses OS-Like Runtime to Unite Reasoning and Action for Robot Navigation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.10787) ⭐️ 8.0/10

NavGPT-3 introduces a hierarchical navigation runtime that connects a long-horizon reasoning language model with a low-latency action policy (NavGPT VLA), scheduling reasoning, acting, and monitoring as separate threads with their own context, tools, and permissions. The 8B NavGPT VLA, trained on 19.28M examples, alone reaches 74.51 SR on R2R-CE, and the full harness sets a new state of the art at 81.51 SR on R2R-CE while matching human performance on RxR-CE (90.43 vs. 90.4 SR). This work shows that the interface between high-level language-model reasoning and low-level physical control is itself a central design problem, not an afterthought, and that an OS-like threading model can make embodied agents more responsive to sudden real-world events. It matters for robotics and embodied AI because it demonstrates a practical path to combining frontier reasoning models with fast action policies, potentially accelerating deployment of autonomous navigation systems. The action policy uses codec allocation to assign visual tokens in proportion to scene change, and the harness reduces minimum reaction time from 3-19 seconds per language-model decision to 0.5-1 second per action-policy step (1-2 Hz). The system runs at about 1 minute 22 seconds per episode on RxR-CE, versus roughly 3 minutes for a human, and the authors plan to release all models, code, and evaluation records.

Vision-language-action (VLA) models, pioneered by Google DeepMind's RT-2, integrate visual perception, language understanding, and low-level action output by fine-tuning a vision-language model on robot trajectory data. ## [Disk-backed KV memory layer enables 50M-token LLM context](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.10845) ⭐️ 8.0/10

A paper tests galahad-kv, a memory layer that saves each ~16,000-token block's KV state to encrypted local NVMe disk and reloads it byte-exact without recomputation. On 50,000,000 tokens of public text served through vLLM on one NVIDIA H100 with Gemma 4 12B and 31B, all 100 probed blocks loaded with no recompute, loading was 2.8-4.3x faster and used 8.8-12.3x less GPU energy than recomputing, and long-range recall accuracy reached 82/100 (12B) and 98/100 (31B). This offers a practical way to give LLMs an effective 50-million-token memory without retraining or architectural changes, directly addressing the context-window bottleneck that limits long-document, codebase, and agentic workloads. The large speed and energy savings over recomputation could make very long-context serving far cheaper on existing single-GPU hardware. This is reuse of stored state rather than a wider attention window: only one block is loaded at a time, answer quality depends on the model, writing the memory is a one-time cost, and the store requires terabytes of local NVMe disk. The authors also describe a test protocol designed to resist common ways of gaming long-context benchmarks and provide a single-GPU reproduction using public software plus a free licence for the package.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 9, 04:00

**Background**: Large language models can only use text that fits in their context window, and they normally recompute the internal key-value (KV) state for a prompt every time it is sent, which is expensive for long inputs. The KV cache stores intermediate attention states so they can be reused instead of recalculated, and prior work has mostly focused on compressing it in GPU memory. vLLM is a high-performance inference engine that manages KV-cache handling and batching, while Gemma 4 is Google's open-weights model family; this paper instead offloads KV state to encrypted NVMe disk to extend effective context.

Researchers present RFChipAgent, a first-of-its-kind multi-agent LLM flow for end-to-end analog/RF circuit design automation, built on four pillars: multimodal RAG with private per-document FAISS indexing, specialized topology/schematic/testbench agents, a closed-loop hybrid sizing engine combining TPE and CMA-ES, and a trust-scored simulation database. The sizing engine evaluates every candidate in a simulator-in-the-loop framework, and the trust-scored simulation database accumulates verified performance data to build an adaptive optimization model that informs subsequent trials. ## [NOMOS compiles written policies into statically verified tool-call gates for LLM agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.11030) ⭐️ 8.0/10

NOMOS, a four-pass compiler, translates natural-language policies into deterministic tool-call gates for LLM agents, using only tool-schema-level static verification (no prover, solver, or LLM verifier) to repair or reject 37% of airline and 13% of retail candidate rules. On the τ²-bench benchmark, the gate reduces policy violations among state-changing calls from 66.3% to 2.6% (airline) and from 30.8% to 6.9% (retail), while achieving zero attack success rate on the banking suite. This work addresses a critical safety problem in tool-using LLM agents, which often silently violate the policies they are deployed to enforce, by providing a lightweight, on-premise compilation approach that avoids heavyweight formal methods and per-action LLM verification. The dramatic reduction in policy violations and the zero attack success rate on banking demonstrate that static verification at the tool-schema level can be both effective and efficient, potentially enabling safer deployment of autonomous agents in high-stakes domains. The compiler's static verification repairs or rejects candidates that would otherwise block the tool satisfying their own precondition or read arguments the tool lacks; without it, most shipped rules are inoperable. Decisions take microseconds without an LLM call, compilation runs on-premise on open-weight gemma-4-26B, and a 26B model's compilation is not significantly worse than hand-written or frontier-compiled rules; however, there is a domain-dependent benign-utility cost, and on three other suites the attack success rate is at most 3.6%.

**Background**: Tool-using LLM agents are increasingly deployed to perform tasks such as booking flights or processing retail orders, but they can violate organizational policies either accidentally or due to adversarial attacks. Prior defenses either hand-write rules, query an LLM verifier for each action, or use heavyweight formal methods like theorem provers, which can be slow or impractical. NOMOS introduces a compiler that turns natural-language policies into deterministic gates checked against tool schemas, ensuring that only compliant tool calls are executed. The τ²-bench benchmark is a standard evaluation suite for tool-agent-user interactions, measuring both task success and policy compliance.

## [Paper Proves LLMs Are Equivalent to Monotone Compression](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.11031) ⭐️ 8.0/10

A new arXiv preprint (2610.11031) theoretically proves that large language models, formally modeled as next-token predictors, are equivalent to monotone (order-preserving) compression algorithms, with the two constructible from each other while preserving the same error up to an additive gap of 2. The paper further shows this equivalence requires monotonicity if and only if cryptographic infinitely-often one-way functions exist, and derives that next-bit pseudoentropy of a distribution is equivalent to its monotone incompressibility. This work provides a formal theoretical foundation for the long-hypothesized link between intelligence and compression, moving beyond prior experimental correlations to a rigorous equivalence. It could reshape how researchers think about evaluating and understanding LLMs, and it yields a cryptographic result of independent interest connecting pseudoentropy and incompressibility. The equivalence holds up to an additive error gap of 2, and the monotonicity requirement is tied to the existence of cryptographic infinitely-often one-way functions, meaning the result has computational hardness implications. The corollary strengthens prior work by Haitner et al. (ITCS'23), which had only shown that incompressibility implies next-bit pseudoentropy, by establishing the reverse direction as well.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 9, 04:00

**Background**: A long-standing hypothesis in AI and neuroscience holds that intelligence is closely related to compression, the ability to represent information efficiently. Recent experimental work supports this: Deletang et al. (ICLR'24) showed LLMs can serve as powerful compressors, and Huang et al. (COLM'24) found LLM compression ability correlates with benchmark performance on knowledge and reasoning. This paper initiates a theoretical study of that connection, using next-token prediction—the standard training objective of modern LLMs—as the formal model of a language model.

## [Nonlinear Attention Explains Inverse-Depth Scaling in LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.11063) ⭐️ 8.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2610.11063) shows that nonlinear attention produces inverse-depth decay of loss across all tested data spectra, in contrast to the power-law depth scaling predicted for linear-attention models. The authors argue that nonlinearity lets attention focus selectively on relevant tokens, so strong and weak spectral directions are learned in parallel rather than sequentially. This work challenges the prevailing power-law scaling theory for model depth and offers a mechanistic explanation for why large language models benefit from depth, which could influence how future models are designed and trained. It also suggests that the global covariance structure of data may be less relevant than previously assumed when attention is nonlinear. The paper links the observed inverse-depth scaling to the central limit theorem: shared error across layers sets a loss plateau, while aggregation of layer-specific differences yields continued gains with depth. The analysis is theoretical and empirical across tested data spectra, but it does not provide a full derivation of the exact scaling exponent.

Large language models, however, use strongly nonlinear attention, which may behave differently.

## [Row Normalization Provably Beats Adam and Muon in High-Dimensional Classification](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.11309) ⭐️ 8.0/10

A new arXiv preprint (2610.11309) proves that row-wise normalization can achieve strictly higher population accuracy than full-batch Adam and exact-SVD Muon in high-dimensional multiclass classification. The advantage stems from row normalization's class-wise Euclidean geometry asymptotically preserving population decision-boundary directions, while Adam's coordinate-wise geometry and Muon's spectral geometry introduce nonvanishing distortions. This theoretical result challenges the common assumption that Adam and Muon are universally superior optimizers, and could influence future optimizer design by highlighting the importance of geometry-preserving normalization. It provides a rigorous foundation for understanding why different optimizers generalize differently despite fitting the same training data. The advantage holds under an isotropic Gaussian-cloud data model and extends to power-law spectra with class-mean exponent below one, even under heavily anisotropic test noise. However, when both class-mean and test-noise covariances are diagonal and sufficiently close, the advantage over Adam can reverse, but applying the same random rotation to both restores it.

This paper provides a theoretical comparison of these optimizers in high-dimensional settings, where the geometry of the learned classifier can significantly affect generalization.

Journals and conferences increasingly screen manuscripts for LLM-written text, but this study shows that benchmark accuracy is only provisional and can collapse the moment a new model generation ships. The findings imply that research-integrity policy must require detectors to be re-verified with every LLM release, including earlier versions, or risk either mass false accusations against human authors or widespread missed AI assistance. In the two simulated screening scenarios covering all 23 versions, screens either flagged one in eight human-written abstracts or missed one in three rewrites of the newest version; a commercial detector missed most rewrites of the version just after the sharpest boundary while flagging almost no human-written abstracts. Vocabulary differences between model versions largely track where detection transfers and where it fails, and detectors trained on later versions can also miss rewrites of earlier ones.

## [Co-Installed Agent Skills Silently Conflict, Benchmarks Miss It](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.11647) ⭐️ 8.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2610.11647) presents the first empirical study of conflicts between co-installed skills in coding agents, mining 822,109 candidate similar-skill pairs from 20,947 repository snapshots and running 312 confirmed pairs across three models (6,368 runs, 169,294 tool calls, 542 agent-hours). It finds that nearly one in four installed skills is co-installed with a skill doing the same job, and that a similar skill takes over one in five runs without lowering task completion. This matters because task-completion benchmarks, the standard way the AI/ML community evaluates coding agents, can pass even when an installed skill's core constraints (such as a ban on touching git) are silently dropped. The findings give agent platform developers concrete guidance: score exclusive core functions, guard the first skill read, and surface which skill actually ran. Conflicts are decided at the first skill read, almost always before any file is changed, and install location determines which skill runs while listing order barely matters; the final reply names the skill used in only 0.9% of substituted runs. A pre-tool hook at that first read restores fidelity on exclusive core functions to the level of runs that open the installed skill first.

**Background**: Coding agents such as Claude Code, Cursor, and Codex can be extended with agent skills: directories containing a SKILL.md file that tells the model when and how to perform a task. Because skills come from independent sources like teams, developers, plugins, and copied collections, an installed skill can end up co-installed with a similar skill doing the same job, and the model chooses between them based only on name and description. ## [LLM Judge Reliability Audit Exposes Severe Verdict Inconsistencies](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.12083) ⭐️ 8.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2610.12083) presents a comprehensive reliability audit of LLM-as-a-Judge, stress-testing six frontier models across four benchmarks, five prompt formats, two presentation orders, three sampling temperatures, and ten repetitions per condition. The authors introduce the Trustworthy Verdict Rate (T), a unified metric capturing the joint probability that an evaluation is reproducible, order-invariant, and accurate. The findings challenge the widespread treatment of LLM judges as deterministic ground truth, showing that verdicts can flip under identical replications and position-order swaps. This has significant implications for NLP evaluation practices, as unreliable judges could undermine benchmark comparisons and model selection across the field. The audit reveals that verdicts change across identical replications even at temperature zero, position-order swaps flip the majority of verdicts on challenging tasks, and the most deterministic judge achieves perfect consistency by trivially repeating incorrect verdicts with only 51% agreement with ground truth. The authors also derive a theoretical upper bound on accuracy imposed by position bias and show that reliability is item-specific rather than model-level.

## [ReSI: Recursive Safety Improvement for Resilient AI Alignment](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.12233) ⭐️ 8.0/10

A new arXiv preprint (2610.12233) introduces ReSI, a recursive safety improvement framework that uses automated research to iteratively red-team, develop training recipes, and update target models. Across four dense and mixture-of-experts models, ReSI cut the mean X-Teaming attack success rate from 86.01% to 31.45%, far below the 56.69% frontier result attributed to GPT-5.6-Luna. The work reframes safety alignment as a continual, recursive process rather than a one-time fix, which matters as models are updated frequently and new red-teaming methods keep exposing fresh vulnerabilities. If validated, this approach could give AI safety researchers a practical path to models that resist known attacks and generalize to unseen risks. In each round, ReSI applies diverse red-teaming methods to find vulnerabilities, develops candidate training recipes, and promotes the update with the largest safety gain among those passing a Pareto gate on capability retention. It reportedly matches or exceeds evaluated frontier models on in-distribution and out-of-distribution safety benchmarks while largely preserving general capabilities, though it remains an arXiv preprint without peer review or community discussion yet.

## [ARGUS: An Evidence-Constrained Agentic Framework for Interpreting Noncoding Variants](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.12281) ⭐️ 8.0/10

Researchers present ARGUS (Agentic Regulatory Genomics for an Uncertainty-aware Scientist), a framework that strictly separates deterministic biological computation from LLM-mediated reasoning by wrapping 458 DNABERT-based transcription factor (TF) binding models in a hypothesis-directed investigation loop. On variant rs6983267 at the 8q24 cancer risk locus, the same planner produced four divergent trajectories for four TFs, with FOXA1 rescued in 3 steps by real ADASTRA allele-specific binding data (15 experiments, FDR = 0.030) and KLF6, RAD21, and SP1 abstaining after 8 steps due to mixed, nonsignificant, or absent direct evidence. Over 90% of disease-associated variants from genome-wide association studies fall in noncoding regulatory regions, yet their functional interpretation remains a central open problem in genomic medicine, and LLMs prompted to interpret such variants routinely hallucinate TF binding changes and fabricate experimental support. ARGUS's evidence-constrained design could improve the reliability of AI-assisted variant interpretation and reduce hallucinations in a domain where incorrect functional claims have direct clinical implications. All observations in the case study come from real ADASTRA, JASPAR, and ENCODE cCRE queries rather than simulated data, and a comparison of fixed-priority versus LLM-mediated planning shows the LLM planner reaches identical verdicts with fewer tool calls by declining evidence that cannot resolve the claim under test. The framework's verifier deterministically interprets each observation, and intermediate results change the investigation path, with the planner selecting evidence sources based on current uncertainty.

## [Predicting Alignment Generalization with Value Representations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.12410) ⭐️ 8.0/10

This paper establishes the new task of alignment generalization prediction, i.e., predicting how fine-tuning a model on one value changes its behavior on held-out values, and benchmarks representational techniques across 66 values from modern alignment targets. It finds that activation-based representations achieve correlations of 0.45 with the generalization matrix, far outperforming textual-description baselines at 0.05. This work matters because post-training on narrow behaviors can unexpectedly shift model behavior in unseen contexts, so being able to predict such spillover effects is critical for safer AI alignment and post-training. It also offers a more empirical, representation-driven approach to designing multi-value alignment targets, which could affect how developers build and evaluate aligned models. The best activation-based methods reach a correlation of 0.45 with the generalization matrix versus 0.05 for description-based baselines, and the learned representations can measure similarity among values in a multi-value alignment target, which correlates significantly with model robustness. The paper also presents initial evidence for a shared, model-independent value space, used to build the first taxonomy of LLM values grounded in empirical generalization dynamics.

It has significant implications for evaluating LLM capabilities, designing AI research tools, and understanding the limits of machine-driven scientific discovery. The study introduces a generative verifier to sustain reasoning strength and avoid 'thought collapse,' and treats the unlearned model's recovery rate as an approximate upper bound on algorithmic innovation ability. Recoverable algorithms tend to be simple in structure or core ideas, while others are less straightforward.

## [Observational Estimator Quantifies Peer-Review Noise at ICLR 2017-2025](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.06591) ⭐️ 8.0/10

A new arXiv paper builds an observational estimator of peer-review decision noise from public review data alone, calibrates it against the NeurIPS 2014 and 2021 consistency experiments, and applies it to nine years of ICLR (2017-2025; 36,113 papers, 134,912 reviews). It estimates that 23-30% of accept/reject decisions would flip under a different committee at k=2 reviewers, and that 30-50% of accepted papers would be rejected. The results quantify how much randomness is baked into top ML conference decisions, which affects authors, reviewers, and program chairs who rely on these outcomes for careers and research direction. It also offers a cheap, reusable method for auditing review noise without running prohibitively expensive duplicate committees. The estimator uses a Bayesian ordered-probit model to decompose scores into paper quality and reviewer noise, then a logistic model to map scores to decisions, simulating two independent committees with B=1,000 posterior draws and committee sizes k=2,3,4. External calibration at NeurIPS 2021 (k=3) yields a simulated disagreement rate of 23.3% [21.7%, 25.0%] versus the reported 23.0% (bias +0.3pp), and internal 2+2 reviewer splits agree within 1pp for 2018 and 2021-2025; no robust time trend in reviewer noise is found, and no LLM attribution is attempted due to lack of post-2022 review text or confidence data.

## [Mooncake: KVCache-Centric Disaggregated Architecture for LLM Serving](https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.00079) ⭐️ 8.0/10

Moonshot AI's Mooncake serving platform for Kimi separates prefill and decoding clusters and builds a disaggregated KVCache pool from underutilized CPU, DRAM, and SSD resources in the GPU cluster. Its KVCache-centric scheduler, combined with a prediction-based early rejection policy, achieves up to a 525% throughput increase in simulated long-context scenarios while meeting SLOs, and enables Kimi to handle 75% more requests under real workloads. This is one of the first detailed public accounts of a production LLM serving system, showing that rethinking KVCache management and prefill/decode disaggregation can yield order-of-magnitude throughput gains for long-context workloads. The techniques are directly relevant to anyone building or operating LLM inference infrastructure, and the paper was recognized as a Best Paper at FAST'25. Mooncake's core is a KVCache-centric scheduler that balances maximizing effective throughput against latency-related SLOs, and unlike prior work it assumes highly overloaded conditions, using a prediction-based early rejection policy to shed load. The reported 525% throughput gain comes from simulated scenarios, while the 75% more requests figure reflects real Kimi workloads.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 9, 04:00

**Background**: Large language model inference has two phases: prefill, which processes the input prompt in parallel and is compute-bound, and decode, which generates output tokens one at a time and is memory-bandwidth-bound. The KV cache stores key-value attention states of previously processed tokens so they don't need recomputation, but its memory footprint grows linearly with sequence length, making long-context serving expensive. Prefill-decode disaggregation runs these two phases on separate hardware so each can be specialized, and Mooncake extends this idea by treating the KV cache itself as the central resource to schedule and cache across the cluster.

## [A PDE Framework for Score-Based Diffusion Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.05940) ⭐️ 8.0/10

The paper develops a PDE framework for score-based diffusion processes associated with the heat flow of a compactly supported data measure, establishing weak well-posedness on positive-time intervals and deriving a sharp one-sided divergence bound for the score. This bound, the Euclidean form of the Li-Yau differential inequality, yields sharp uniform L^p-stability estimates for the generative Fokker-Planck equation and proves convergence in 2-Wasserstein distance at rate sqrt(t) as t approaches 0+. This work provides rigorous mathematical foundations for the stability and consistency of score-based diffusion models, which have achieved empirical success but lack complete theoretical understanding. The results clarify how exact-score dynamics concentrate on the data support without necessarily recovering the data distribution, offering a mathematical perspective on the balance between imitation fidelity and generative diversity. The convergence holds for both deterministic and stochastic generation, for positive terminal densities with finite absolute entropy and second moment; in the deterministic case, almost every trajectory converges to a point of the data support, and for empirical data a trajectory-wise square-root rate is obtained. An explicitly solvable case identifies limiting weights and their dependence on Gaussian initialization, while a relative-entropy estimate quantifies the effect of score approximation.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 9, 04:00

**Background**: Score-based diffusion models are a class of generative models that learn to reverse a noising process by estimating the score (gradient of the log density) of the data distribution, often formulated via stochastic differential equations. The Fokker-Planck equation is a partial differential equation describing the time evolution of a probability density under drift and diffusion, and it governs the dynamics of these models. The Li-Yau differential inequality is a classical result in geometric analysis that bounds the gradient of positive solutions to the heat equation, providing Harnack inequalities and heat kernel estimates.

A new arXiv paper (2603.25015v2) reports that system prompt instructions which cooperate in English compete in Spanish despite identical semantic content, an effect the authors call 'instruction topology inversion.' The study used a corpus of 22 hand-authored probes tested against a production system prompt decomposed into 56 blocks, with statistical significance established via permutation testing. The authors note that the topology inversion is mediated by social register — the imperative mood carries different obligatory force across speech communities — and that models trained on multilingual data have learned these conventions, though the exact models and languages beyond the four tested are not specified in the abstract.

The authors trained over 150 VLMs on 34 LLMs spanning 7 model families under a strictly controlled recipe, validating the law on more than 200 textual and 50 multimodal benchmarks. ## [Resource Hijacking: A New Threat Class for LLM Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15108) ⭐️ 8.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2608.15108v2) identifies and systematically studies "resource hijacking" in LLM agents, where attackers induce agents to misuse high-value resources such as external APIs, GPUs, servers, and deployment or approval workflows without directly obtaining those resources or their credentials. The authors introduce ResourceHijackBench, an executable benchmark with 300 attack scenarios and 900 attack prompts across six resource categories, and propose ResGate, a pre-execution resource authorization defense. The work shows that preventing direct access to resources is insufficient, since agents can still be manipulated into using those resources on an attacker's behalf, with attack success rates of 70.0% to 89.6% across four model backends and 84.1% on the OpenClaw harness. As LLM agents become increasingly connected to valuable infrastructure, this overlooked threat class has significant implications for agent framework developers, security teams, and enterprises deploying autonomous workflows. Resource hijacking achieves attack success rates 62.4 to 84.0 percentage points higher than direct resource acquisition across the four model backends, and among three existing defenses evaluated, the lowest average ASR is still 55.1%. The proposed ResGate defense combines model-based resource-use extraction with deterministic policy enforcement based on trusted requester identity metadata, reducing the average ASR on OpenClaw to 23.6%.

A new arXiv paper (2609.14193) shows that on-policy distillation (OPD) training on just 8 real prompts achieves performance comparable to training on a 17k-problem dataset, and proposes a data-free OPD (DF-OPD) setting where the system generates its own training questions. With only 64 self-generated questions and no seed examples, DF-OPD matches full-data OPD in single-teacher settings, and in multi-teacher OPD across mathematics, code, and instruction following, 1k generated questions match roughly 7k real post-training examples. ## [Once: A CLI Tool That Caches Command Output](https://github.com/alex0ptr/once) ⭐️ 7.0/10

Once is a Go-based CLI utility that runs a command in the current directory, prints its stdout, and caches the result in a small per-user background daemon. Repeated calls with the same command, directory, and tenant key are served from memory until the TTL expires, so secrets from tools like 1Password can be read without approving every access with a fingerprint. This matters because it addresses two pain points in modern developer workflows: redundant execution of slow or expensive commands, and the friction of repeatedly authenticating secret reads when working with AI agents. By caching outputs in a daemon, Once makes agent-driven workflows smoother while keeping secrets off disk. The cache is keyed on the command, working directory, and tenant key, and entries expire after a configurable TTL; the tool is written in Go and runs as a per-user daemon. A key limitation is that users must prefix commands with "once" to benefit from caching, which some community members find inconvenient.

## [Small LLM agents struggle to use wall-clock time budgets productively](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.10833) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2610.10833) evaluates whether small LLM agents can operate under explicit wall-clock time budgets, testing Qwen3.6-27B on five MLE-Bench Lite competitions and Qwen3-4B on Zork I from the Jericho benchmark. It finds that when budgets are only stated in the prompt, agents fail to translate them into controlled time use, and proposes harness-based timing feedback and GRPO reinforcement learning with budget-aware rewards as interventions. As agentic systems are increasingly deployed with real-world runtime and cost constraints, the ability to respect and productively use time budgets becomes a practical requirement rather than a nice-to-have. This work shows that current small LLM agents lack this capability, and that even successful budget adherence does not automatically translate into better task performance, pointing to a key open problem for agent designers. Injecting timing information through the harness substantially improved budget adherence for Qwen3.6-27B without measurable performance loss, and enforcement hooks tightened adherence further; GRPO-based RL achieved near-perfect adherence on Zork I and generalized to held-out budgets, but did not improve MLE-Bench task performance. Notably, RL-trained policies learned when to stop but often filled extra time with repeated actions, and multi-budget GRPO training tended to collapse toward the strategy learned for the shortest budget.

## [Self-Supervised Keyframe Discovery Enables Horizon-Invariant Behavior Cloning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.10857) ⭐️ 7.0/10

The paper introduces Keyframe Mnemonics, a self-supervised method that discovers information-critical observations (mnemonics) by learning an objective from randomly sampled past observations and using it as a reward for keyframe selection. It then trains a behavior cloning policy conditioned on these keyframes, achieving 100% success on synthetic memory domains and a 13.9% average absolute improvement over the strongest baseline across 23 robot manipulation tasks. This work addresses a fundamental limitation in behavior cloning for long-horizon, non-Markovian tasks, where recurrent models suffer from hidden-state collapse and attention models are bounded by context length. By providing context retention guarantees over an infinite horizon with a small set of keyframes, it could significantly improve imitation learning for robotics and other sequential decision-making domains. The method is fully self-supervised, requiring no manual keyframe annotations or privileged information, and under certain task-structure assumptions it provides context retention guarantees over an infinite horizon. On a real robot, it retains 80% success rate at 20x longer horizons, though the approach relies on task-structure assumptions that may limit generality.

**Background**: Behavior cloning (BC) is a simple imitation learning approach where a policy is trained to mimic expert actions from demonstrations. In non-Markovian environments, the optimal action depends on long histories, not just the current state, so policies must remember past observations. Existing architectures use recurrent networks (which can suffer from hidden-state collapse and unstable gradients) or attention mechanisms (which are limited by fixed context length) to handle this, but both have drawbacks for very long horizons.

## [LLMs Fail at Learning Community Norms Through Interaction, Paper Finds](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.10906) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper introduces a multi-agent community debate setting where access to debate is governed by synthetic norms, in order to study normative competence in LLMs independently of pretraining exposure. The authors show that baseline LLM agents fail to learn norms even when doing so would improve their accuracy, and that adding normative modules yields inconsistent results highly sensitive to norm style and the underlying model. This is the first work to operationalize and evaluate normative competence in LLMs, a central AI alignment challenge as autonomous agents are increasingly deployed in human communities governed by fast-changing, often arbitrary norms. The finding that current systems excel at behavioral mimicry but cannot discern socially enforced order has direct implications for AI safety, multi-agent coordination, and the reliability of LLM agents as social partners. The paper reports an 'unselective attribution failure': when idiosyncratic, non-normative behaviors accompany the true norm, LLM agents indiscriminately copy the idiosyncratic noise alongside enforced rules, and this pattern persists even when imitating unnecessary behaviors is explicitly penalized. Norm-following was found to be highly sensitive to both the style of norm and the model powering the normative module, suggesting a lack of generalizability.

## [StoreBench: A Live-Commerce RL Environment for Training and Evaluating LLM Operator Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.10942) ⭐️ 7.0/10

Researchers introduced StoreBench, a live-commerce simulation in which an LLM agent runs a mid-size online apparel store on a production-grade commerce backend, acting through the same 29 merchant tools a human operator would use. In evaluations of seven frontier LLMs across 11 scenarios (30-45 days plus a full simulated year) and three world seeds, no model matched the scripted smart-triage policy on average — the best, DeepSeek-V4-Pro, passed only 49% of task-seed cells versus the heuristic's 97% — while a GRPO post-training run lifted Qwen3.5-27B's mean composite on held-out tasks from 0.136 to 0.373. Most agentic benchmarks are static, with rewards delivered as terminal verdicts and pass bars set arbitrarily, so StoreBench's dynamic, calibrated, and hack-resistant design offers a more realistic way to measure and improve long-horizon economic decision-making in LLM agents. Its finding that human experts still outscore every model (mean composite 0.708 vs. 0.700) highlights how far autonomous operator agents remain from reliable real-world deployment. The environment uses a windowed operation budget that makes simulated time a function of actions taken, so model latency cannot influence simulated time, and every episode replays identically given a sequence of actions. Pass thresholds are calibrated against scripted anchor policies and the reward is hardened against a catalogue of reward hacks; the authors release five example training-split tasks, ten sample trajectories, and scoring/verification tooling, but withhold the full environment and evaluation suite to keep the benchmark uncontaminated.

## [Paper Models LLM Agent Context Curation as Capacitated Assortment Problem](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.11007) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv preprint (2610.11007) formulates the curation of always-loaded context files such as AGENTS.md as a capacitated assortment problem with censored feedback. It proves an upper bound on optimal file size regardless of candidate instruction count, and shows that appending every instruction with positive standalone value can be arbitrarily worse in net value than selecting an optimal subset. Context files are a growing pain point in LLM agent design, since every loaded token is re-charged in each session round and larger files can degrade model compliance. This work gives curators theoretical guidance on when to add or remove instructions, potentially changing how agent context files are maintained in practice. Feedback is inherently censored: the benefits and harms of loaded instructions are observable, but missing instructions only generate feedback when their absence causes harm. The paper shows that deleting instructions ignored by agents can inevitably remove helpful ones, characterizes how much evidence should be collected before adding an instruction, and bounds regret when human reviewers can inspect only a limited number of edits per period.

**Background**: LLM agents typically load a fixed context file, such as AGENTS.md or CLAUDE.md, at the start of every session to configure their behavior. In practice, human or automated curators usually grow these files by appending new instructions, but each token is charged again in every later round and oversized files can hurt performance. The paper borrows tools from capacitated assortment optimization, a classic operations research framework for choosing a limited set of items under a capacity constraint, and from censored-feedback learning, where outcomes are only partially observed.

## [Balancing Reference Guidance and Free Generation in Reasoning RL Rollouts](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.11128) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2610.11128) derives a closed-form KL divergence that quantifies how much reference guidance to give during trajectory rollouts for reasoning RL, showing the divergence decreases with the product of the probability of generating a different correct trajectory and the reference surprisal. Based on this analysis, the authors propose Adaptive Reference Guidance (ARG), a prefix selector learned from continuation outcomes that is applied to all-failure groups in GRPO, achieving the highest aggregate pass@12 on Qwen3-4B and Qwen3-8B across five mathematical reasoning benchmarks. This work addresses a key bottleneck in reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) for LLMs: when all sampled trajectories in a group fail, training signal vanishes, and reference solutions can help but may reduce exploration diversity. By providing a principled way to decide how much reference guidance to use, ARG could improve sample efficiency and reasoning performance in GRPO-style pipelines without extra generation or success-probability estimation. The analysis shows that continuation success alone does not determine the optimal amount of guidance, because a longer prefix tends to raise the probability of generating a different correct trajectory but lowers the reference surprisal (the negative log probability of the reference suffix given the prefix). ARG learns a prefix selector shared across training questions from continuation outcomes, constructs correct trajectories within a fixed generation budget, and is applied to all-failure groups in GRPO; experiments cover five mathematical reasoning benchmarks with Qwen3-4B and Qwen3-8B.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 9, 04:00

**Background**: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) trains reasoning models by sampling multiple trajectories per question and rewarding those that pass verification, often using Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO). A common failure mode is the all-failure group, where every sampled trajectory is wrong and no learning signal is produced; one remedy is to seed rollouts with a prefix of a verified reference solution. KL divergence measures how one probability distribution differs from another and is widely used in RL to quantify the cost of deviating from a reference policy, while prefix continuation refers to letting a model generate a completion starting from a given reference prefix.

## [Lower Reconstruction Loss Can Hurt: DRQ Refines Low-Bit LLM Quantization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.11226) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2610.11226v1) shows that minimizing reconstruction loss in weight-only post-training quantization (PTQ) does not necessarily improve downstream task performance, and can even degrade it on the same calibration data. The authors propose Distributionally Robust Quantization (DRQ), a post-hoc refinement that minimizes worst-case reconstruction loss over a constrained set of input activation distributions, improving models quantized by six representative PTQ methods including AWQ, GPTQ, and ParoQuant. This challenges a foundational assumption of most weight-only PTQ pipelines, which treat reconstruction loss as the primary optimization target, and suggests that widely used methods like AWQ and GPTQ may be leaving accuracy on the table. Because DRQ is a post-hoc refinement that adds no inference overhead and works across dense and mixture-of-experts LLMs, it could be broadly adopted to improve low-bit deployment without changing existing quantization grids or operators. DRQ refines the integer codes representing quantized weights within the existing quantization grid, keeping quantization parameters and inference operators unchanged, so it adds no inference overhead. The method is motivated by the finding that weights with lower calibration reconstruction loss can have higher loss when the input activation distribution shifts, and it is validated across six PTQ methods and both dense and mixture-of-experts models.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 9, 04:00

**Background**: Post-training quantization (PTQ) compresses a trained LLM's weights to low bit-widths (e.g., 4-bit or lower) after training, typically using a small calibration dataset, so the model fits in less memory and runs faster. Most weight-only PTQ methods, such as AWQ and GPTQ, choose quantized weights by minimizing reconstruction loss—the difference between the original and quantized layer outputs on calibration data. Distributionally robust optimization (DRO) is a framework that optimizes for the worst-case data distribution within an uncertainty set, rather than assuming the calibration distribution matches deployment. DRQ combines these ideas by treating input activation distributions as uncertain.

Researchers introduce Harness Compilation (HC), an offline procedure that adapts how work is divided between a frozen small vision-language model (≤9B parameters) and its external harness, using a large teacher's execution traces to revise reusable content and control. Across seven visual question-answering settings, HC improves scores over bare students by 9.9–23.9 points without any weight updates or teacher calls at deployment. This offers a practical path to boost small VLM performance in resource-constrained deployments without retraining or expensive inference-time teacher calls, which matters for edge and cost-sensitive multimodal applications. It also reframes harness design as a measurable allocation problem rather than a uniform removal of decisions. Interventions on five runtime decision types (invocation, selection, argument generation, evidence integration, and abstention) show that requesting evidence and generating open queries can be costly, while bounded choices and reading supplied text remain useful student work. Fact cards benefit all ten evaluated students, but decision policies transfer unevenly, and recompilation helps when the transferred interface no longer fits; with 100 practice items, HC exceeds answer-only LoRA on three tasks.

Harness Compilation uses a large teacher model to observe student execution traces offline and revise the harness, so that at deployment the frozen student runs with a harness tuned to its actual capabilities.
