A new arXiv paper (2608.09202v2) proposes CRUISE, an uncertainty-aware cross-modal sensor fusion framework that integrates a vision-language model (VLM)-guided uncertainty quantification module to produce fine-grained, pixel-level uncertainty estimates for autonomous driving perception. The framework also introduces a dynamic adaptive mechanism that explicitly models cross-modal dependencies to better exploit the complementary nature of multi-sensor inputs. Robust cross-modal fusion remains a critical bottleneck for autonomous driving because sensor reliability varies dramatically across poor visibility and adverse weather, and existing uncertainty-aware methods rely on coarse feature-level estimates that fail to generalize in out-of-distribution scenarios. By leveraging VLM prior knowledge and contextual reasoning for pixel-level uncertainty, CRUISE could improve perception robustness in exactly the challenging conditions where current systems are most likely to fail. The key technical novelty is replacing simple feature-level uncertainty estimates with VLM-guided pixel-level uncertainty, which provides a more informative guide for the fusion process, combined with an adaptive mechanism that captures cross-modal dependencies. As an arXiv preprint, the work has not yet undergone peer review, and no community discussion or benchmark results are provided in the available material.

Researchers introduced EconSkills, a skill library and evaluation framework that distills verified EconWebArena trajectories into parameterized standard operating procedures (SOPs) for retrieving live economic data. Each skill records its scope, navigation procedure, site-specific guidance, verification checks, and recovery steps while replacing source-instance values with placeholders. Web agents often revisit the same sites, yet most evaluations discard procedures learned in earlier successful interactions, so this work addresses the underexplored problem of skill transfer and retrieval. It offers a concrete design target for match-aware selection and context delivery, which could improve agent efficiency and generalization for web automation researchers. In controlled transfer, matched skills improve success over no-skill prompting and require fewer steps on paired successes, and the parameterized skill prompt substantially outperforms the corresponding raw-trajectory prompt. With the full 50-skill library, retrieval is competitive with the no-skill baseline overall and performs best on tasks with a direct family match, while approximate matches on other tasks offset these gains.

## [DENSE Distills Agent Trajectories into Shortcut Trees for Self-Refinement](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.21423) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (arXiv:2609.21423v5) introduces DENSE (Distilling Evidence from Nested Subtask Executions), which organizes trajectory-derived evidence into nested shortcut trees by consolidating redundant attempts, identifying resolved subtasks, and retaining useful steps alongside outstanding requirements. The authors also design REFIT to measure success-rate changes between an initial attempt and feedback-guided retries, and report that DENSE achieves the highest strict pass rate among feedback methods without external outcome supervision across four agent models on Terminal-Bench 2.1, improving over initial attempts by 7.12–21.81 percentage points with 19.0–43.6% fewer agent tokens on retries. Online agent deployments accumulate massive, diverse execution trajectories for which predefined annotation criteria hardly exist, so extracting reusable experience typically requires costly manual annotation or verifier signals that fail to scale. DENSE shows that reusable, evidence-grounded feedback can be distilled from the trajectories themselves without post-execution rewards or correctness labels, which could make continual agent self-improvement far more practical at scale. DENSE processes the shortcut tree bottom-up, fusing consecutive attempts under one parent into a shortcut that retains failed approaches, a compact working path supported by observations, the final local outcome, and source references, while unresolved shortcuts keep unmet requirements and relevant observations. On hard tasks, DENSE consistently outperforms self-reflection in cumulative pass rate across multiple feedback iterations on all four models, though the work remains an arXiv preprint without community discussion.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 9, 04:00

**Background**: LLM agents following ReAct-style reason-act-observe loops generate long execution trajectories that are valuable for debugging, evaluation, and training, but most are redundant, incomplete, or failed. Trajectory distillation typically compresses such traces into smaller student models or reusable knowledge, while self-refinement methods like Self-Refine let a model iteratively critique and improve its own output. DENSE combines these ideas by turning noisy traces into structured, evidence-grounded feedback that agents can use to retry the same task without any external reward or correctness label.

## [Type-Safe Models Follow Option Names, Not Definitions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.26758) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2609.26758v3) shows that typed decision models can be misled by option names: when only the name-definition mapping is changed while the question, state, and text stay identical, decision-flip rates are up to 70.4 percentage points higher with yes/no names than with a 0/1 control. With yes/no names, reassignment also drops mean AUC from 93.8% to a below-chance 23.2%, even though the type-error rate stays at 0%. This finding matters because output-type correctness is often treated as a guarantee of reliable structured decisions, yet the study shows type-safe outputs can still fail to follow explicit option definitions. It affects anyone deploying typed decision models in automation, evaluation, or safety-critical pipelines, and suggests option naming is an overlooked source of decision instability. The experiments cover 1200 decision tasks with task-specific definitions across Jev and two open-weight models, and the yes/no versus 0/1 gap holds across all 4 binary decision rules. Random strings used as option names produce flip rates close to neutral controls across all three models, supporting option-name polarity rather than reassignment alone as the driver of instability.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 9, 04:00

**Background**: Typed decision models return structured results such as a selected option name, and each option pairs a name with a definition that specifies its intended meaning. Jev is a proprietary System One decision model from TypeSafe AI, released in limited early access on 15 September 2026. AUC (area under the ROC curve) is a standard metric where 100% means perfect ranking and 50% is chance level, so a below-chance 23.2% indicates systematically inverted decisions.

## [READ-Bench: Benchmarking Historical Case Retrieval for Time-Series Diagnosis](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.32123) ⭐️ 7.0/10

READ-Bench is a new benchmark that evaluates historical-case retrieval for time-series diagnosis across 12 multivariate datasets, defining relevance by shared fault or event type rather than signal shape. It compares classical distances, symbolic retrievers, self-supervised and foundation-model embedders, and their fusion, plus label-aware and language-model rerankers, under one protocol varying supervision, pollution, and corpus scale with significance testing. Retrieval in time-series diagnosis has typically been judged only indirectly through downstream prediction, so this benchmark provides the first direct, standardized evaluation of how well systems find historically relevant fault cases. Its finding that pretrained representations offer no statistically detectable advantage over strong classical baselines could redirect effort toward reranking and supervision rather than ever-larger embedding models. Under a common channel-independent interface, the decisive factor is a small amount of resolved-case supervision at reranking: a Gaussian-process reranker that propagates a few neighbor labels in embedding space outperforms more sophisticated representations and language-model reasoning, and holds under pollution and at full corpus scale. The authors' final system fuses a normal-residual-scored embedder with a dynamic time warping leg via reciprocal-rank fusion, then reranks with the Gaussian-process reranker, improving NDCG@10 on all 12 datasets by +0.11 from reranking and +0.16 over the strongest single base retriever.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 9, 04:00

**Background**: Time-series diagnosis systems monitor multivariate sensor data to identify faults, and historical-case retrieval means finding past episodes with the same fault type to support the current diagnosis. Classical retrievers use distance measures like dynamic time warping, symbolic retrievers convert signals into discrete symbols, and self-supervised or foundation-model embedders learn general representations from large unlabeled corpora. Reranking is a second stage that reorders an initial candidate list, often using extra labels or a language model.

## [Training-Free Latent-Space Constraint Cuts Reasoning Overthinking](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.34181) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv preprint (2609.34181v2) proposes a training-free framework that uses a quadratic program to project deviating hidden states back into a concentrated latent region where efficient reasoning steps naturally cluster. Experiments on four models (1.5B to 14B) across six benchmarks in math, coding, and scientific QA show up to 12.1% accuracy improvement while reducing generated tokens by 11.8% to 52.8%. Overthinking is a major cost driver in Large Reasoning Models, and existing fixes like keyword suppression or length forcing often truncate necessary steps and cause underthinking. A training-free method that cuts token costs without sacrificing accuracy could be widely adopted for cheaper inference, and the latent-space perspective may inspire new efficiency research directions. The method is training-free and model-agnostic, requiring no fine-tuning or reinforcement learning, and code is released at github.com/hzn18/Opt4Reasoning. However, it is an arXiv preprint without peer review or community validation, and the quadratic program introduces per-step projection overhead whose net latency impact is not fully characterized in the abstract.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 9, 04:00

**Background**: Large Reasoning Models (LRMs) are LLMs trained to produce long chains of thought, which improves accuracy on hard tasks but often leads to overthinking — generating redundant steps that waste tokens and compute. Hidden states are the internal vector representations a model computes at each layer, and latent space refers to the high-dimensional space these vectors inhabit. Quadratic programming (QP) is a mathematical optimization technique that minimizes a quadratic objective subject to linear constraints, commonly used to find the closest valid point to a given input.

## [FlowState Treats Execution State as Memory for Long-Horizon LLM Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.34565) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2609.34565v2) proposes FlowState, a framework that treats an agent's execution state as reusable memory, storing semantically typed state nodes, their relations, and references to raw tool observations. Using Incremental State Update (ISU) and Progressive State Access (PSA), it improves average success rate on MemoryArena by 4.55 points and average pass rate on τ³-Bench by 13.95 points versus a full-context baseline with the same DeepSeek-V4-Flash model, while cutting token consumption by 43.2% and 40.6%. Long-horizon agent tasks force a trade-off between retaining full history (expensive) and compressing it (lossy), and FlowState shows both accuracy and cost can improve simultaneously. This matters for researchers and practitioners building agent systems that must run many steps with tool calls, where context cost and lost details are persistent bottlenecks. FlowState separates persistent retention from on-demand access: ISU maintains the current state from new inputs and feedback within a single execution loop, while PSA progressively reveals historical states and supporting evidence during reasoning. The reported gains come from a single model (DeepSeek-V4-Flash) and two benchmarks, so generalization to other models and task domains remains to be validated.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 9, 04:00

**Background**: LLM agents solve tasks by repeatedly reasoning, calling tools, and observing results, and as tasks grow longer the accumulated history can exceed context limits or become very costly. Common approaches either keep the full context or compress it, but compression is lossy and the relevance of old information often only becomes clear later. FlowState instead stores structured state nodes with typed semantics and references back to raw observations, so details can be retrieved when needed rather than kept in context at all times.

## [EvolvingNav: Predictive 4D Belief for Navigation in Changing Worlds](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.39166) ⭐️ 7.0/10

The paper introduces EvolvingNav, a predictive 4D belief framework that lets embodied agents navigate evolving worlds by modeling target persistence and relocation from timestamped 3D object histories. It also releases EvoWorld-Bench, a benchmark of 54 scenes and 803,680 tasks grounded in human activity traces, and reports improved navigation success and search efficiency in both simulation and real-robot experiments. Most spatial-memory navigation systems assume the world stays static between visits, so they fail when targets move unobserved. EvolvingNav's principled persistence-relocation model and event-driven belief updates could make service, warehouse, and home robots far more reliable in real environments where objects and people constantly move. The belief distinguishes persistence at the last observed location from relocation to alternative locations and retains probability mass outside the known candidate set, while negative observations downweight hypotheses using calibrated, visibility-conditioned detection probabilities. A frozen, zero-shot vision-language controller consumes the updated belief to choose actions and replan, and ablations show the clearest gains under learnable temporal patterns and when uncertainty is preserved.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 9, 04:00

**Background**: Persistent spatial memory allows embodied agents to remember where objects were seen on previous visits, but remembered locations become stale when targets move while unobserved. Evolving-World Navigation formalizes this problem: agents must infer target locations from intermittent observations, predict where targets will be at inspection time, and revise beliefs as new visual evidence arrives. The 4D belief here means a time-indexed probabilistic representation built from timestamped 3D object histories, rather than a static map.

## [Paper Defines and Detects 'Empty Commitments' in AI Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01045) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2610.01045v2) formally defines 'empty commitments'—promises of future action that an AI agent cannot possibly fulfill given its tools and runtime—and introduces a validated checker plus a controlled benchmark of 293 follow-up requests across five setups. The checker, validated against 400 human labels, reveals that four open-weight models of 8-14B parameters fail on 45.9% of responses when no tool exists, while a frontier model fails on 4.4% but still makes promises without the enabling call. This work addresses a practical safety and reliability gap in agentic AI: agents that promise actions they cannot perform, which can mislead users and erode trust in deployed systems. By providing a formal definition, taxonomy, and detection method, it offers a foundation for evaluating and mitigating this failure mode before deployment or at runtime. The paper defines empty commitments on top of commitment semantics with three failure types, an anchoring condition for promises a tool could make real, and an outcome taxonomy separating failures from honest deferrals and over-refusal. Telling the model its runtime cuts open-weight failures nearly in half where nothing is doable but changes nothing where a scheduler exists; a directive capability card removes most failures at the cost of over-refusal, while running the checker in the loop and rewriting flagged replies removes more at a smaller cost.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 9, 04:00

**Background**: In AI agent research, 'commitment semantics' refers to the formal study of promises and obligations that agents make, often drawing from multi-agent systems where commitments have lifecycles and normative force. Unlike a broken promise, an empty commitment is decided by the agent's configuration at the moment of speaking—if no tool or runtime mechanism exists to carry out the promised action, the promise is empty from the start. This paper builds on that tradition to create a setup-blind detector that can flag such promises from a single turn, before deployment or at runtime.

## [Causal Memory Policy Fixes Retrieval Positivity Violation in Memory-Augmented LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02070) ⭐️ 7.0/10

The paper introduces Causal Memory Policy (CMP), a causal inference framework that intervenes on retrieval itself by reserving a fixed number of context slots for memories sampled with known propensities, enabling identification of memory utility in memory-augmented LLMs. It proves the causal factorization of memory utility through retrieval, the unbiasedness and exact variance of a self-normalized inverse propensity weighting estimator, and the optimal decision rule under irreversible operations. This work exposes a fundamental flaw in current memory-augmented LLM systems: when a memory is never retrieved, its utility is unidentifiable, and this failure affects 54% of required memories on LongMemEval and 67% on LoCoMo, persisting even in deployed systems. CMP improves discrimination between required and non-required memories from 0.54 to 0.66 AUC, offering a principled solution for building more reliable long-term memory in LLMs. The paper shows that identified memory utility alone is insufficient for retention decisions: per-query utility reaches 0.78 AUC on the query for which it is estimated, yet no aggregation available to a retention policy predicts a memory's value on unseen queries. Code is available at an anonymous repository.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 9, 04:00

**Background**: Memory-augmented large language models store past information and retrieve relevant memories to improve task performance, but deciding which memories to retain is challenging. Causal inference typically relies on the positivity assumption, which requires that every subgroup has a non-zero probability of receiving each treatment; violations occur when some treatments are never observed. In memory systems, a retrieval-level positivity violation arises because memories that are never retrieved cannot have their utility estimated from store-level interventions.

## [BudgetAPO: Noise-Adaptive Prompt Optimization for Tight API Budgets](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.05671) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper introduces BudgetAPO, a single-stage prompt optimizer that dynamically sizes its evaluation slices based on each task's measured noise, rather than using fixed-size minibatches. Across seven benchmarks and five subject models, BudgetAPO ranked first on every subject and beat every baseline under Holm-corrected paired tests, returning the seed prompt in only 13% of runs at 250 calls versus 86% for GEPA. Most existing automatic prompt optimization methods assume hundreds to thousands of model calls, which is impractical behind paid, rate-limited APIs; BudgetAPO directly addresses this gap for practitioners with constrained budgets. Its noise-adaptive evaluation strategy could become a standard component for making prompt optimization viable in cost-sensitive production settings. BudgetAPO combines three components: a noise-adaptive rule that sizes the evaluation slice using a short probe, a fixed slice that turns every accept/reject decision into a paired comparison, and a reflective operator that jointly rewrites reasoning strategy and output format. On GPT-OSS-20B, GEPA needed five times as many calls to match BudgetAPO's 100-call score.

**Background**: Automatic prompt optimization (APO) adapts large language models without updating their weights by automatically searching for better natural-language prompts. Prior methods such as OPRO (Optimization by PROmpting) and GEPA (Genetic-Pareto Prompt Evolution) iteratively generate and evaluate candidate prompts, but typically require hundreds to thousands of subject-model calls. Under tight budgets, multi-stage pipelines can exhaust the budget and return the seed prompt unchanged, while single-stage methods compare candidates on fixed-size minibatches regardless of task noise.

## [Self-Referenced Social Preferences Enable Cooperation Without Peer Rewards](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07881) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper introduces self-referenced social preferences, in which each agent learns a model of its own reward and applies it to other agents' observed transitions to estimate their outcomes from its own perspective. The authors evaluate two integration methods—modifying the learning reward or weighting policy updates—on three sequential social dilemmas (Escape Room, Clean Up, and Commons Harvest), showing that agents learn cooperation without observing peers' private rewards, even where independent learners fail. This work removes a key assumption in prior social-preference MARL research—that agents can access peers' reward signals—making cooperative multi-agent learning more realistic for settings where rewards are private. It could influence how researchers design cooperative agents in domains like autonomous systems, resource sharing, and human-robot interaction, and it suggests that social preferences can be grounded purely in observed behavior. The effective integration point depends on the social preference: inequity aversion works best when incorporated into the reward together with a value look-ahead, whereas a purely benevolent preference benefits from policy-update weighting. Under partial observability, the policy-update approach continues to support cooperation, and the method frequently achieves more equitable divisions of jointly produced returns than agents with access to true rewards.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 9, 04:00

**Background**: Multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) studies multiple learning agents sharing an environment, each pursuing its own reward, and often evaluates social metrics such as cooperation and equity. Social preferences—such as inequity aversion or benevolence—are utility functions that account for others' outcomes and can promote cooperation, but prior approaches typically require agents to observe peers' rewards. Sequential social dilemmas are temporally extended environments, analogous to repeated Prisoner's Dilemma games, where cooperation and defection are properties of policies rather than single actions.

## [Self-Retrospection Distillation Turns Hindsight into Foresight for RLVR](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.08077) ⭐️ 7.0/10

The paper introduces Self-Retrospection Distillation (SRD), a method that distills post-hoc trajectory experience into pre-interaction foresight predictions of the same policy. Across 10 tool-integrated reasoning and long-horizon agentic tasks, SRD complements RLVR and self-distillation baselines with gains of up to 24.2 percentage points, and in a 2B setting where 98% of rollout groups are all-failure, it lifts success from 0.0% to 60.6% under the same rollout budget. This work addresses a core weakness of group-relative RLVR: when all rollouts in a group receive identical rewards, the learning signal vanishes even though trajectories contain useful information. By recovering learning signal from reward-uniform groups, SRD could make RLVR training far more sample-efficient and effective for hard reasoning and agentic tasks where failures dominate. SRD treats foresight as a training target only, so it need not be explicitly generated at inference time, adding no inference overhead. Its advantage is most pronounced when reward contrast is scarce: 37–98% of rollout groups are reward-uniform across model scales, and the 2B all-failure case shows the method still extracts signal from sampled trajectories.

Knowledge distillation, meanwhile, transfers knowledge from a teacher to a student and is increasingly combined with RL to improve reasoning post-training.

## [Learn2Play Bench Tests LLM Agents' Learning from Experience](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.08215) ⭐️ 7.0/10

The paper introduces Learn2Play Bench, a benchmark of newly designed text-based games with novel or counterintuitive rules that require LLM agents to acquire knowledge through interaction rather than relying on pretrained knowledge. It provides reproducible feedback and automatic scoring, and varies game instances to test whether agents can transfer what they learn to new situations. Existing benchmarks mostly evaluate tasks whose rules are given in instructions or already familiar to pretrained models, making it hard to separate genuine learning from reasoning with existing knowledge. By isolating learning from experience in unfamiliar environments, this benchmark offers a cleaner way to measure and improve LLM agents' adaptability, which matters for researchers building agents that must operate in dynamic real-world settings. The study evaluates how backbone models, self-evolving methods, and agent harnesses affect learning ability, yielding three findings: retaining complete records of actions and feedback supports better learning than summarizing them into rules or strategies; top human players achieve higher peak scores and explore more varied strategies with fewer repeated actions; and with the backbone fixed, changing the harness can improve performance while reducing estimated inference cost.

## [ParanoiaEval: Benchmarking Unnecessary Defensive Work in Coding Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.08662) ⭐️ 7.0/10

Researchers introduced ParanoiaEval, the first benchmark for unified evaluation of risk-treatment capabilities in coding agents, grounded in the Avoidance-Transfer-Mitigation-Acceptance framework from software engineering risk management. It contains 200 evidence-controlled repository-level task pairs drawn from 50 repositories, where each pair differs only in a single piece of treatment-defining evidence, plus dedicated metrics for risk-treatment violations and evidence responsiveness evaluated by a human-calibrated agentic judge. This work establishes risk treatment as an independent capability dimension of coding agents, showing that stronger task capability does not guarantee more appropriate risk treatment and that unnecessary defensive work occurs in 11.2%–58.7% of runs despite explicit evidence. It gives researchers and practitioners a systematic way to diagnose and improve agent behavior that directly affects developer experience. The benchmark operationalizes the four fundamental risk treatments for coding-agent settings and uses a human-calibrated agentic judge for reliable evaluation; large-scale experiments covered 8 representative models plus a post-hoc human study. Notably, agents exhibit systematic patterns consistent with established human risk-management findings, suggesting that knowledge from human practice can guide diagnosis and improvement of this capability.

## [Study: Agent Skills' Utility Depends on Content and Configuration](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.08875) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new empirical study on 87 SkillsBench tasks compares the same Agent Skills across nine model-harness configurations, finding that identical Skills help some configurations and hurt others on 36.78% of tasks. The authors also retrieve candidates from a corpus of 37,596 marketplace Skills and show that reranking by support for required operations raises first-choice pass rates by 4.35–5.80 percentage points. The findings challenge the common assumption that adding a relevant Skill automatically improves agent performance, showing that utility is conditional on content, execution configuration, and how multiple Skills are organized. This gives agent developers concrete guidance on evaluating operation support, allowing procedure adaptation, and making artifact dependencies explicit when building Skill-based systems. The study derives 17 authoring practices linking executable procedures to recovery, preservation of task requirements, and checks on final artifacts, and finds that Stage Plan and Dependency DAG organization outperform use order alone, with DAG's extra benefits concentrated in tasks supplied with five or six Skills. Relevance rankings were also found to overlook more useful candidates, and the analysis combined LLM-assisted review of content, execution traces, and final artifacts with author verification.

## [Humanize Enforces Judgement Boundaries in Agentic Coding](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.08900) ⭐️ 7.0/10

Humanize introduces a multi-agent orchestration workflow for agentic coding that enforces explicit, mechanically gated judgement boundaries between planning, implementation, review, and learning, using deterministic hooks and cross-vendor reviewer agents. Over 68 versions in 108 days, it gathered 1,468 GitHub stars and was validated through 118 public postmortems and applications including a 567-file gem5 build-system migration and top-three finishes in the MLSys 2026 FlashInfer contest. This work addresses the critical reliability gap in agentic coding: the agent that writes code is a poor judge of whether it is done, so Humanize's cross-vendor review and mechanical gates offer a practical methodology for improving AI-assisted software development. Its real-world deployment and public postmortems provide valuable evidence for teams building or adopting multi-agent coding workflows. Humanize enforces 72 mechanical gates and routes work between roles via deterministic hooks rather than a model; viewed as a Markov chain over repository states, alternating builder and reviewer samples jointly from two models, so a defect survives only if both miss it. The postmortems reveal that independent review catches unsupported builder claims, but stopping remains a key weakness—two thirds of rounds occurred after implementation was accepted—and the evidence is observational, not a controlled comparison.

Researchers introduced Policy Learning with a Language Bottleneck (PLLB), a framework where AI agents generate linguistic rules that capture high-level strategies behind rewarding behaviors. PLLB alternates between a rule generation step guided by language models and an update step where agents learn policies guided by those rules, and it was tested across five diverse tasks including a two-player signaling game, maze navigation, image reconstruction, and robot grasp planning. The framework addresses a key weakness of modern AI systems like self-driving cars and game-playing agents, which achieve superhuman performance but often lack human-like generalization, interpretability, and interoperability with users. By letting agents share learned rules with humans, PLLB could enable more effective human-AI coordination and more trustworthy decision-making systems. PLLB works even when a single rule is insufficient to describe an entire complex policy, and the authors provide source code at https://github.com/meghabyte/bottleneck. The paper has been accepted to TMLR 2026, indicating peer-reviewed validation of the approach.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 9, 04:00

**Background**: Reinforcement learning agents typically learn policies through trial and error, producing behaviors that are effective but hard for humans to understand. A "language bottleneck" means the agent must compress its strategy into natural-language rules, forcing the policy to be expressed in human-readable terms. Language models are used to generate these rules because they can produce fluent, general descriptions of behavior. This combination aims to make learned policies both interpretable and transferable to new situations.

## [Normative model reveals ramping vs rhythmic attention strategies](https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.07440) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2501.07440v3) presents a normative model of a signal detection task in which attention is metabolically costly, showing that optimal attention allocation is temporally structured in one of two patterns: it ramps up as evidence accumulates when attention costs penalize intense focus, but fluctuates rhythmically when costs are less prohibitive. ## [CAFÉ: Causal Black-Box Testing for Machine Unlearning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.16525) ⭐️ 7.0/10

Researchers introduced CAFÉ, a causal black-box testing method that detects persistent feature influence in machine unlearning by intervening on a feature, propagating the change through downstream features, and checking whether model predictions still respond. On two causal-network benchmarks with four unlearning methods, CAFÉ achieved 0.92–0.93 pairwise accuracy in ranking residual influence, compared with at most 0.71 for existing checks. Machine unlearning is increasingly required for privacy and compliance, but approximate unlearning can leave hidden influence that existing direct-input checks miss. CAFÉ provides a more reliable black-box verification method, which matters for auditors, regulators, and engineers who must certify that a deployed model no longer depends on removed data or features. CAFÉ treats the model as a black box and uses only its predictions, measuring residual influence through both direct and indirect causal paths and providing fine-grained diagnostics of which channels and subgroups still carry influence. The paper reports that existing checks fail in both directions: they certify models whose influence persists through downstream features and flag correctly unlearned models.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 9, 04:00

Because unlearning is usually approximate, its effectiveness must be tested, but testers often lack access to model parameters, training history, or the unlearning procedure. Black-box testing, also called specification-based testing, evaluates a system only through its inputs and outputs, while causal inference studies how changes in one variable affect another. Features complicate testing because even after a feature is removed from a model's inputs, its influence can persist through downstream features.

By reusing step-level candidates across diffusion-sampled trajectories, this work offers a modular alternative to monolithic unified hybrids and could make test-time scaling cheaper and more effective for reasoning-heavy tasks. The pipeline separates exploration (diffusion sampling) from evaluation (PRM scoring) and solution synthesis (final solver), and ablations show the final solver is critical for converting stitched but imperfect rationales into accurate answers. ## [mAVE Binds Audio-Video Watermarks to Prevent Splicing Attacks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.07090) ⭐️ 7.0/10

Researchers introduced mAVE (Manifold Audio-Visual Entanglement), a training-free watermarking framework for native joint audio-visual diffusion transformers that binds audio and video watermarks to a shared generation session using a cryptographic digest. Experiments on LTX-2 and MOVA report a 99.8% true-positive rate and 0% observed false-positive rate in swap tests, retaining 99.2% TPR under FrameAvg temporal averaging. Existing audio and video watermarks can each be individually valid yet originate from different generation sessions, letting an adversary splice them together and falsely attribute the pair to a vendor's original joint output. mAVE closes this provenance gap, which matters for copyright protection and trustworthiness as joint audio-visual generative models become more capable and widely deployed. mAVE separates public record retrieval from secret session authentication: a fixed public index locates the server record while a randomized payload binds audio bits to a session-keyed video grid via a cryptographic digest. Verification is provider-assisted and uses one prompt-conditioned joint inversion without modifying generator weights or training auxiliary watermark networks, with analysis covering distribution preservation, routing/clipping budgets, and local-perturbation bounds.

## [IAD-Unify: Unified Architecture for Industrial Anomaly Understanding, Segmentation, and Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.12440) ⭐️ 7.0/10

Researchers present IAD-Unify, a unified architecture that connects a multimodal language model (Qwen3.5), a dense visual expert (multi-reference DINOv2), and a diffusion editor (Stable Diffusion) through task-specific token interfaces. The model achieves 73.02% MMAD Macro_7, the highest listed public segmentation AP average of 57.10% with one reference, and the lowest Controlled masked DINO distance of 0.3765, while also introducing the Anomaly Evidence dataset of 54,501 deduplicated industrial images. This work shows that understanding, pixel-level segmentation, and controlled image generation for industrial defects can be handled by one shared parameter set without forcing every task through the same visual bottleneck, which could influence how future multimodal industrial inspection systems are designed. It also provides a large, quality-controlled dataset and benchmark results that may accelerate research in automated defect inspection. A multi-reference DINOv2 pathway compresses a dense anomaly field of 1,369 cells into 81 structured evidence tokens consumed by Qwen3.5, while a separate 256-query interface resamples Qwen states into Stable Diffusion's cross-attention context; evidence tokens are deliberately excluded from the generation pathway. Staged optimization initializes dense evidence, aligns it with language, calibrates segmentation, and then pretrains and specializes the diffusion editor while preserving earlier capabilities.

**Background**: Industrial anomaly inspection requires three complementary capabilities: explaining a defect in language, localizing its pixels, and synthesizing a controlled edit. DINOv2 is a self-supervised vision transformer commonly used as a backbone for dense computer vision tasks, Qwen3.5 is a native vision-language model, and Stable Diffusion is a diffusion-based text-to-image model whose cross-attention context can be steered by external representations. IAD-Unify combines these components so that one shared model can perform all three inspection tasks without conflating their inputs, supervision, or outputs.

## [SparKV adaptively streams or computes KV cache to speed on-device LLM inference](https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.21231) ⭐️ 7.0/10

SparKV is an adaptive KV cache loading framework that decides per KV chunk whether to stream it from the cloud or compute it locally on the device, overlapping the two execution paths to cut latency. Experiments across diverse datasets, LLMs, and edge devices show it reduces Time-to-First-Token by 1.3x-5.1x with negligible quality loss and lowers per-request energy by 1.5x-3.3x. On-device LLM inference is bottlenecked by the expensive prefill stage that builds the KV cache, so offloading part of that work to the cloud while keeping computation local could make edge AI far more responsive and battery-friendly. This matters for phone, laptop, and embedded deployments where users expect fast first responses without draining the battery. SparKV models the cost of individual KV chunks and refines offline-generated schedules at runtime to rebalance communication and computation under fluctuating wireless connectivity and edge resource availability. The reported gains come with negligible impact on response quality, though the approach depends on network conditions and cloud availability.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 9, 04:00

**Background**: Large language models generate text in two phases: a prefill phase that processes the entire input prompt in parallel and builds a Key-Value (KV) cache, and a decode phase that generates output tokens one at a time using that cache. The KV cache stores attention keys and values so the model does not recompute them for every new token, but its memory footprint grows with context length, making prefill costly on resource-constrained devices. Time-to-First-Token (TTFT) measures the delay from sending a request to receiving the first output token, and it is dominated by the prefill stage.

## [APEX: Assumption-free Embedding Metric for Image Quality Assessment](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.07786) ⭐️ 7.0/10

Researchers introduced APEX (Assumption-free Projection-based Embedding eXamination), a new image quality assessment framework that uses Sliced Wasserstein Distance as a mathematically grounded, assumption-free similarity measure. APEX is embedding-agnostic and employs the open-vocabulary foundation models CLIP and DINOv2 as feature extractors, and benchmarking shows it is more robust to visual degradations than established baselines like FID. Traditional metrics such as FID suffer from a closed-vocabulary bottleneck and rigid parametric assumptions, which can misrepresent the quality of modern generative models. APEX offers a more stable and robust evaluation alternative, potentially improving how the generative modeling community compares GANs, diffusion models, and other image synthesis systems. APEX inherits scalability to high-dimensional spaces, as proven with theoretical and empirical evidence, and exhibits intra- and cross-dataset stability for reliable out-of-domain evaluation. However, it remains a specialized arXiv preprint without accompanying community discussion, so its practical impact is yet to be validated.

**Background**: FID (Fréchet Inception Distance) is a widely used metric that compares feature distributions of real and generated images using a pretrained Inception-v3 network, but it relies on outdated closed-vocabulary features and assumes Gaussian distributions. Sliced Wasserstein Distance is an optimal-transport-inspired measure that compares high-dimensional distributions by projecting them onto one-dimensional subspaces, making it computationally tractable and free of parametric assumptions. CLIP and DINOv2 are open-vocabulary foundation models that provide rich, general-purpose visual features, which APEX uses instead of Inception features.

## [FeatCal: Closed-Form Feature Calibration for Merged Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.13030) ⭐️ 7.0/10

FeatCal introduces a layer-wise feature calibration method that reduces the performance gap in merged models by minimizing feature drift using a small calibration set and closed-form weight updates, with no gradient descent or extra modules. On CLIP-ViT-B/32 Task Arithmetic, it achieves 85.5% versus 77.0%/78.8% for Surgery and ProbSurgery, and on FLAN-T5-base GLUE it reaches 85.2% versus 83.7%/82.2%. Model merging is a cheap way to combine task-specific experts into one model, but merged models often underperform the original experts; FeatCal closes much of this gap efficiently, which could make merged models more practical for deployment. Its sample efficiency and speed (256 examples per task in 53 seconds, about 4x faster than baselines) make it attractive for researchers and practitioners in AI/ML. FeatCal uses a closed-form solution to update weights layer by layer in forward order, reducing feature drift while staying close to the merged weights; it requires no gradient descent, iterative optimization, or extra modules. On CLIP-ViT-B/32, only 8 examples per task reach 82.9%, demonstrating strong sample efficiency.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 9, 04:00

**Background**: Model merging combines the weights of multiple fine-tuned task experts into a single model without joint training or retraining, but the merged model often underperforms the individual experts. Feature drift refers to the difference between features produced by the merged model and by the expert on the same input, and it can propagate through layers and degrade final outputs. FeatCal addresses this by calibrating the merged model layer by layer using a small calibration set, leveraging a theoretical decomposition of feature drift into upstream propagation and local mismatch.

## [EEG Foundation Models Evaluated Beyond Clean Accuracy](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.17562) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv study evaluates six EEG foundation models (EEG-FMs) and a supervised baseline across ten datasets along three axes: robustness to test-time perturbations, interpretability via attribution methods, and expressiveness through pooling and probing analyses. It finds that no single model dominates all failure modes, that attribution maps concentrate on task-appropriate brain regions, and that poor head-only performance is largely explained by pooling strategy rather than weak pre-trained representations. This work challenges the prevailing practice of judging EEG-FMs solely by clean, in-distribution accuracy, showing that conclusions about model quality depend heavily on evaluation choices. It offers actionable recommendations—report robustness per perturbation type, produce attribution maps, and test multiple pooling strategies—that could reshape how the AI/ML and neurotechnology communities benchmark future EEG foundation models. The most noise-robust model is among the most fragile under channel dropout, and much of the dropout fragility disappears when channels are removed rather than zero-padded. Block-wise probing and attention analysis reveal that late blocks are repurposed during fine-tuning while early blocks already hold task-related information, and EEG-FMs show sufficient representational capacity when token-level embeddings are preserved.

## [SAGE: Self-Evolving Framework Boosts Spatial Reasoning in VLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.18162) ⭐️ 7.0/10

Researchers propose SAGE (Spatial Alignment via Geometric Evolution), a self-evolving framework that integrates geometric and linguistic duality consistency into GRPO training to improve robust spatial reasoning in vision-language models. SAGE co-evolves duality generation and solution, using a dynamic operation pool that identifies challenging operations and retires mastered ones, and is model-agnostic and data-efficient compared to prior post-training methods. Vision-language models often answer original inputs correctly but fail under valid spatial transformations, revealing a gap between instance-level correctness and robust spatial reasoning. SAGE addresses this fragility and could benefit researchers in multimodal reasoning, reinforcement learning, and applications like robotics and embodied AI that depend on reliable spatial understanding. SAGE encourages coherent answers across original and transformed inputs by incorporating duality consistency into GRPO training, and it can be applied as a lightweight adaptation stage to any existing VLM. Experiments on video and spatial reasoning benchmarks show consistent improvements over strong baselines and enhanced generalization to unseen data.

GRPO (Group Relative Policy Optimization) is a reinforcement learning method that reduces compute compared to PPO by comparing groups of responses instead of training a separate value model. Geometric duality is a principle in projective geometry where points and lines swap roles, and SAGE uses this idea to generate transformed inputs with predictable answer mappings.

## [ToBAC: First Backdoor Attack Targeting Unified Autoregressive Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.19227) ⭐️ 7.0/10

Researchers introduce ToBAC (Token by Token Backdoor Attack), the first backdoor attack targeting unified autoregressive models (UAMs), which generate text and image tokens in a single autoregressive pass. The attack uses inconspicuous words like "cool" as triggers that propagate malicious effects across both text and image modalities, achieving a 55% success rate on the Liquid model with model access and 63.1% against JanusPro via data poisoning without model access. This research reveals a new class of security vulnerability unique to unified multimodal architectures, where shared parameters and a single multimodal vocabulary allow a single trigger to corrupt multiple output modalities simultaneously. As UAMs become more prevalent for flexible multimodal generation, this finding highlights urgent safety risks for developers and users of such models, since fabricated content can appear more authentic when text and images are jointly manipulated. ToBAC explores both data-based and model-based poisoning strategies, and with model access a subtle word such as "cool" can induce modality-aligned brand promotion or ideological influence in 55% of generations. Without model access, the attack can be induced through data poisoning, achieving an average success rate of 63.1% against JanusPro, and the code is publicly available on GitHub.

Backdoor attacks implant activatable triggers into models to induce attacker-specified outputs, and while such attacks have been studied in unimodal and multimodal large language models, their behavior in unified autoregressive architectures had not been explored before this work. ## [Distillation Game Paper Proposes Adaptive Evaluation and PoE Defense](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.22737) ⭐️ 7.0/10

An arXiv paper (2605.22737v4) models distillation attacks as a minimax game between a utility-constrained teacher and an adaptive student, deriving an adaptive evaluation rule and a forward-pass-only defense called Product-of-Experts (PoE). Empirically, adaptive students recover substantially more capability on GSM8K and MATH than passive evaluation suggests, narrowing the apparent robustness gap between expensive defenses and PoE. This work suggests that existing anti-distillation defenses may be overestimated because they are judged against passive attackers, and that progress should instead be measured against adaptive students. It matters for model providers who must balance releasing useful outputs against protecting proprietary capabilities via APIs. PoE combines the teacher with a proxy student during generation using a cheap proxy for example value, requiring only a forward pass and thus being substantially cheaper than expensive defenses while preserving higher-quality reasoning traces. The paper notes that strong distillation remains difficult to stop, and code is available at https://github.com/ysfalh/distillation-game.

Product-of-Experts (PoE) is a machine learning technique proposed by Geoffrey Hinton in 1999 that combines several simpler distributions into one, and here it is adapted as a defense that mixes teacher and proxy-student outputs during generation. A minimax game is a standard framework for modeling adversarial interactions where one side maximizes utility while the other minimizes it.

## [TRQAM Stabilizes Off-Policy Fine-Tuning of Flow Policies](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.27079) ⭐️ 7.0/10

This paper introduces Trust Region Q Adjoint Matching (TRQAM), a stable off-policy fine-tuning algorithm that adaptively controls the path-space KL divergence between fine-tuned and pretrained flow policies via projected dual descent. The authors prove that a trust-region parameter λ inside the flow policy's sampling process exactly weights the path-space KL in the stochastic optimal control objective, and on 50 OGBench tasks TRQAM achieves 68% overall success in offline RL versus 46% for the strongest baseline. Off-policy reinforcement learning of pretrained flow policies has been notoriously unstable because small critic errors can be exponentially amplified, often causing performance collapse. By tightly bounding deviation from the pretrained policy within a prescribed KL budget, TRQAM offers a principled fix that could make critic-guided fine-tuning of flow and diffusion policies reliable for robotics and generative control. The method adapts a trust-region parameter λ inside the sampling process of the flow policy and proves that λ exactly weights the path-space KL in the SOC objective, enabling tight control of deviation from the pretrained policy within a prescribed KL budget. Experiments cover both offline RL and offline-to-online RL across 50 OGBench tasks, consistently outperforming prior methods.

**Background**: Flow matching is a generative modeling technique that learns to transport noise into data (or action) distributions via continuous-time dynamics, and it has become a powerful paradigm for generalist robot policies that imitate action chunks. Q-learning with Adjoint Matching (QAM) recast policy improvement for such flow policies as a stochastic optimal control problem guided by a learned critic, but it inherited the fragility of critic-guided improvement. A new arXiv paper (2605.27381v3) develops an oracle-relative computability model with mutable solvers, evaluators, and improvers, showing that uniform simulation keeps every total decision procedure produced by effective self-revision over an oracle A within the class C(A) = {D : D ≤_T A}. It also provides a constructive worked model of Boolean rule acquisition with a sharp teacher-query bound and a terminating protocol that allows revisions to the query proposer. This work offers a rigorous theoretical framework for reasoning about the limits of self-improving AI systems, separating acquisition, certification, and computability ascent. The learned solver can dispense with the teacher on every input while remaining in the same computability layer, but uniformly constructing the required feature-span specification from arbitrary effective feature programs is already as hard as the relative halting problem. As LLM agents increasingly rely on large external skill libraries, this risk directly affects the reliability and safety of tool-using agents, and the benchmark is likely to shape future research on safe skill retrieval and reranking. The benchmark pairs each query with a helpful skill and a same-capability sibling that violates a requirement, using Recall to track helpful hits, HSR to track exposure of the conflicting sibling, and CleanHit to require a helpful hit without that exposure. Across a fixed mixture of 1,235 held-out queries, the four retrievers achieve Recall@3 of 0.903–0.944 but still show HSR@3 of 0.344–0.393; the authors also find that truncating long skills can remove the passages where the two skills' contracts differ, and increasing the reranker's input budget from 512 to 4,096 tokens reduces source-task sibling-first errors by 8.27 percentage points.

The paper introduces S4oP, the first systematic operator-level pruning method for S4 and S4D state space models, using incremental structured masking interleaved with fine-tuning while jointly monitoring accuracy and inference latency. Experiments show that pruning up to 70% of model operators preserves original performance in most cases while substantially reducing inference latency. This work addresses a key barrier to deploying SSMs on resource-constrained devices such as edge hardware, where their computational and memory demands have been prohibitive. By demonstrating that structured operator pruning is an effective and previously unexplored strategy, it opens a practical path for bringing SSM-based sequence models into real-world efficiency-critical scenarios. The method progressively prunes operators by interleaving structured masking with fine-tuning inside a unified training and evaluation framework that enables systematic exploration of efficiency-accuracy trade-offs. The headline result is that up to 70% of operators can be removed with preserved performance in most cases, though the abstract does not specify per-dataset degradation or exact latency numbers.

## [SC-GRPO: Self-Conditioned Credit Assignment for RLVR](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18810) ⭐️ 7.0/10

This paper proposes SC-GRPO (Self-Conditioned GRPO), a method that conditions a model on its own verified trajectories to compute a per-token KL divergence, which is then used as a multiplicative weight on GRPO gradients. Across five benchmarks spanning math, code, and agentic tasks, SC-GRPO outperforms GRPO by 8.1% and DAPO by 5.9%, while also beating On-Policy Distillation (OPD). Token-level credit assignment in RLVR has previously required external resources such as process reward models, ground-truth answers, or external teachers, which limits applicability in pure RLVR settings. By deriving dense per-token supervision entirely from the model's own verified rollouts, SC-GRPO removes these dependencies and could make reasoning-focused RL training simpler and more self-contained for LLM post-training pipelines. The authors prove that distilling from a self-teacher constructed from verified trajectories leads to infeasible weighted-average solutions when multiple verified trajectories exist, which motivates using the KL divergence as a multiplicative weight rather than a distillation target. The method also reports stronger out-of-distribution performance, though the abstract is truncated and full experimental details are not visible.

On-policy distillation (OPD) instead provides dense token-level supervision from a teacher, typically an external model, while on-policy self-distillation uses privileged information such as the correct solution.

## [NCAM: Identifiable Unsupervised Multi-Sensor Regression Under Sensor Bias](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.22200) ⭐️ 7.0/10

The paper introduces the Neural Conjugate Aggregation Model (NCAM), a hierarchical Bayesian framework that combines neural networks with conjugate Gaussian inference to perform unsupervised multi-sensor regression when ground-truth labels are unavailable during training. NCAM learns source-specific bias and reliability conditioned on contextual covariates, resolves structural non-identifiability via sensor anchoring and variance regularization, and integrates locally adaptive Monte Carlo conformal prediction to produce heteroscedastic prediction intervals with finite-sample coverage guarantees. This work addresses a practical and challenging problem in sensor networks, simulation ensembles, and scientific monitoring systems where supervision is costly or infeasible, offering both improved predictive accuracy and well-calibrated uncertainty compared to unsupervised baselines such as mean aggregation, probabilistic PCA, and Kalman filtering. By providing identifiability guarantees and decomposed epistemic and aleatoric uncertainty, it could advance sensor fusion and uncertainty quantification in safety-critical applications. NCAM yields an analytically tractable posterior over a latent target variable by exploiting conjugate Gaussian inference, and its conformal prediction component provides coverage guarantees under exchangeability assumptions. Experiments on synthetic and real-world air-quality datasets show improved accuracy and calibrated uncertainty relative to unsupervised baselines.

**Background**: Multi-sensor regression aims to estimate a latent target from multiple noisy measurements, but sensors often exhibit heterogeneous biases and reliabilities, and labeled ground truth may be missing. Hierarchical Bayesian models place priors on group-level and sensor-specific parameters, while conjugate priors enable closed-form posterior updates. Identifiability ensures that distinct parameter values produce distinct data distributions, which is crucial for interpretable unsupervised learning. Conformal prediction is a distribution-free method that wraps any predictor to produce prediction sets with guaranteed marginal coverage.

## [Reward Observability and the Limits of Offline Checkpoint Selection in RSSM World Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01736) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper studies the closed-loop behavior of a recurrent state-space model (RSSM) world model trained on human demonstrations in Gymnasium's LunarLander-v3, showing that a model-based A2C policy trained in imagination reaches a mean return of +189.5, matching the best model-free A2C checkpoint (+183.7) with roughly 65x fewer real training transitions. The authors introduce the Reward Observability Fraction (ROF), a measure of the Euclidean fraction of the reward gradient in the observable subspace of the linearized latent dynamics, and find that neither ROF nor any of 108 offline summaries can reliably predict the closed-loop collapse of model-predictive control (MPC). This work provides concrete evidence that model-based reinforcement learning with world models can achieve comparable performance to model-free methods at a fraction of the real-environment interaction cost, which is critical for domains where data collection is expensive or dangerous. It also highlights a fundamental open problem: offline metrics, including the newly proposed ROF, fail to predict when a learned world model will catastrophically fail in closed-loop control, underscoring the need for better model validation tools. The ROF depends on how the latent is scaled, so raw levels are not comparable across models; forcing the reward head onto the posterior-corrected latent z raises ROF, and this rise survives a coordinate-invariant check on the two runs tested. The study also finds that MPC collapse varies between training runs with identical data and configuration, and none of the 108 offline summaries screened passes a permutation test, with the best candidate failing on new runs.

## [ACID Adds Cycle Action Consistency to World-Model Planning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.02403) ⭐️ 7.0/10

ACID introduces cycle action consistency, a decision-time planning cost that penalizes predicted transitions whose backward-inferred action (via an inverse dynamics model) does not match the action originally conditioned on. The per-step residual is folded into the planning cost with a scale-invariant adaptive weight, and across four action-conditioned world models and eight tasks in simulation, visual navigation, and real-robot manipulation, ACID consistently improves planning while matching baseline accuracy with substantially less planning compute. Standard planning costs only check how close a predicted terminal state is to the goal, so a world model can produce trajectories that look plausible yet are not physically realizable, causing the real rollout to drift. By explicitly checking transition realizability, ACID offers a general, model-agnostic fix that could make decision-time planning with learned world models more reliable and cheaper for embodied AI and model-based reinforcement learning. The consistency signal comes from an inverse dynamics model that infers the action backward from a predicted transition, and the resulting residual is combined with the standard goal-distance cost using a scale-invariant adaptive weight rather than a fixed hyperparameter. The method is validated on four action-conditioned world models and eight tasks, including real-robot manipulation, and reportedly matches baseline accuracy with substantially less planning compute.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 9, 04:00

**Background**: Action-conditioned world models are learned simulators that predict future states or observations given a candidate action sequence, and they are widely used for embodied control. In decision-time planning, the model is queried at each step to score candidate action sequences by rolling them out and comparing the predicted terminal state with the goal. An inverse dynamics model does the opposite of a forward world model: given a state transition, it infers which action produced it, which is why it can be used to check whether a predicted transition is actually achievable.

## [Study Finds High Answer Conformity Across 105 Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.12796) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv preprint (2607.12796v3) analyzes 105 language models from over twenty labs on 96 single-word prompts, finding that models chose 'serendipity' 46% of the time when asked to pick a word, and that in 28 of 96 categories a single answer accounted for at least 80% of responses. The study introduces an 'answer-choice surprisal' metric, measured as the average -log2 probability of a model's answers under the pooled answers of all other models, and reports that heavily post-trained assistants from major labs are the most conformist while lightly post-trained and persona-tuned models are the most divergent. The findings highlight a systematic lack of diversity in language model outputs, which could affect creative tasks, benchmarking, and applications that rely on varied responses. The concentration being at least as strong among major-lab models suggests that scale and heavy post-training may be driving homogenization rather than diversity, raising concerns about monoculture in AI-generated content. The study used exact match scoring with no embeddings or LLM judge, asked each prompt eight times per model, and found that models avoiding the modal answer mostly land on the same runner-up; against human norms, the field was more concentrated than people in 18 of 20 shared categories. Release order showed no panel-wide trend once model tier was controlled, though GPT, Gemini, Grok, and Qwen became more conformist across releases while Claude's generation-5 releases reversed this trend.

## [CPR Routes Tokens Between Base LLM and Fine-Tuned Expert to Curb Forgetting](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.30158) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv preprint (2608.30158v3) proposes CPR (Critical-Point Routing), a token-level routing framework that keeps the original base LLM for general capability and selectively invokes its supervised fine-tuned (SFT) expert only on 'critical tokens' where the base model fails but the expert succeeds. A lightweight hierarchical router estimates the expert-call probability per token, paired with momentum smoothing and threshold gating at inference; across diverse model-domain configurations CPR reportedly beats the SFT expert by 1.4-5.5% in domain performance while cutting the general-capability drop from 3.4-14.5% to at most 0.5%, invoking the expert on only about one-third of tokens. Catastrophic forgetting is a central obstacle to deploying domain-adapted LLMs, and most prior work mitigates it by modifying the SFT loss, which forces an inherent domain-generality trade-off. CPR sidesteps that trade-off at the model level, suggesting a practical path to domain specialization without sacrificing general ability, which could influence future work on domain adaptation, routing, and continual learning. The router is trained specifically on critical tokens and is described as lightweight and hierarchical, with inference combining momentum smoothing and threshold gating; the reported overhead is minimal because the expert is invoked on only about one-third of tokens. As an arXiv preprint, the results have not yet undergone peer review, and the abstract does not detail which base models, domains, or evaluation benchmarks were used.

## [Perfect Aliasing Can Make Truth Probes Score Below Chance](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.10739) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2609.10739) introduces 'perfect aliasing,' a fitting-label ambiguity where a truth probe trained on compliant contexts cannot distinguish the true bit from the task-prescribed answer, because the two labels are identical there. In a reward-trained Gemma-2-9B policy that always answers falsely on rival trials, an ally-fitted probe scores 0.006 ± 0.005 AUROC at the final layer, while mixed-fit probes score 1.000 on the same held-out activations, showing the truth remains linearly recoverable. This work challenges a common interpretation of truth probes as deception monitors: a below-chance score does not necessarily mean the model hid or stopped representing the truth. It matters for AI safety and interpretability researchers who use linear probes to audit deceptive language models, since it shows such readouts can be artifacts of label ambiguity rather than evidence of concealment. The main experiments use a single-token game that states the secret bit in the prompt, so the recovered direction may simply read a retained copy of it; where the model must infer the bit, no tested arm deceives reliably. Mixed fitting also uses more examples and labelled rival data, so the result shows the true bit remains linearly recoverable rather than proving that separating labels alone explains the gain.

## [HIL-UMI Enables Robot-Free Human-in-the-Loop Post-Training of VLA Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20659) ⭐️ 7.0/10

The paper introduces HIL-UMI, a policy-guided Universal Manipulation Interface (UMI) framework that performs human-in-the-loop post-training of vision-language-action (VLA) models without executing the policy on a physical robot. During handheld UMI demonstrations, it queries the current policy on the same observation stream and uses an Energy Score to compare human and policy action trajectories, triggering data collection when the discrepancy indicates an out-of-distribution state. A separate feedback loop uses low online advantage predictions to refine a progress-based advantage estimator, which then guides advantage-conditioned behavioral cloning on a balanced mixture of base demonstrations and new policy data. Adapting large VLA models to specific deployments is bottlenecked by static demonstration data and imitation objectives that cannot distinguish useful progress from less useful behavior, while interactive post-training normally requires repeated physical robot execution and human intervention. By decoupling data collection from robot deployment, HIL-UMI offers a more scalable path to VLA post-training across operators and locations, which is directly relevant to robotics and embodied AI researchers. Experiments on four real-world tasks spanning long-horizon and precise manipulation show consistent improvement over supervised fine-tuning (SFT), with gains from both targeted collection and advantage refinement. HIL-UMI also outperforms HG-DAgger on the Clean Up Table task while requiring lower per-frame collection time, though the evaluation is limited to four tasks and does not yet demonstrate broad generalization.

Researchers introduced MemCalib, a benchmark grounded in realistic memory-system scenarios that evaluates whether an LLM gives each in-context memory an appropriate degree of influence over its response. Testing frontier open- and closed-source models revealed systematic over-use or under-use of memory, and experiments with GRPO and on-policy self-distillation showed a directional skew where models improve in one direction while degrading in the other. MemCalib-RL was evaluated across model families and scales including Qwen3-8B, Ministral-3-8B-Instruct, and Qwen3.5-35B-A3B, achieving the best overall performance while better balancing over-use and under-use, with gains generalizing to external benchmarks. MA-JEPA introduces a stochastic world model for multi-agent reinforcement learning that replaces observation reconstruction with self-supervised prediction of target representations, using a categorical latent state and a causal Transformer trained with posterior and action-conditioned dynamics objectives. In experiments on SMAC, it matches or exceeds the strongest reported comparator mean win rate on four of eight evaluated maps. The architecture uses a training-only joint predictor that conditions on all agents' local states and actions to predict each agent's next local observation embedding, and these predictions pass through the same local posterior used during real interaction, with a centralized critic used only for value learning. A new arXiv paper (2610.03827v2) demonstrates that similarity scores used as evidence of shared structure between models and brains or across languages can be misleading when the underlying structure is removed or the measurement instrument fails. Across 17 languages, a grammaticality probe transfers worse between distant languages (r = -0.66), but the probe's own accuracy also falls along the same axis and is at chance in four languages, four of which are among the five most distant. Counting 272 language pairs as independent yields p = 0.0006 for a steering effect that becomes null (p = 0.155) when the 17 languages are the unit of analysis. In brain alignment, a training objective raises a language model's similarity to fMRI responses from 0.10 to 0.34 (reliability ceiling 0.54), yet targets with the brain correspondence destroyed still reach 0.31, and a shuffled target scores about k/n against the real one for rank k and n sentences.

It leverages the calibrated confidence that decision models such as Jev attach to each decision to derive expected output quality and tuple prices without any labeled data. Existing semantic query systems either apply a fixed threshold per operator or tune accuracy per operator, ignoring how errors propagate through joins. This framework could influence how query optimizers for ML-based predicates select plans and set accuracy targets, benefiting both the database and ML communities. The paper shows accuracy is plan-invariant under pointwise-deterministic policies, that selection pushdown is not quality-sound when escalation bands are calibrated on the plan's own candidates, and that expected quality can be computed in polynomial time under bag semantics. Choosing which tuples to drop is NP-hard, but the optimization decomposes into per-tuple decisions via two Lagrange multipliers, with confidence-centric skipping avoiding scoring tuples that can no longer affect the target.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 9, 04:00

**Background**: Semantic query engines evaluate predicates using machine-learned models rather than exact conditions, so the choice of query plan affects not only cost but also the result. Calibrated confidence means a model's stated probability of correctness matches its observed accuracy, which lets the system estimate expected error per decision. Jev is a decision model from TypeSafe that returns a choice, score, or yes/no probability for a given application state, rather than acting as a chatbot.

## [Stackelberg Game Model Analyzes When AI Defenses Are Sufficient](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09892) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2610.09892v2) formally analyzes when feedback-driven AI defenses—from automated testing, human red teaming, and incident response—provide sufficient protection. It proves that a finite attack surface is defended with probability 1 under conditions of persistent discovery, effective repairs, and protection-preserving updates, and formulates a defender-led Stackelberg game to characterize economically optimal investment in proactive discovery and reactive repair. This work provides formal mathematical foundations for an under-theorized but critical problem in AI security: how much to invest in finding versus fixing vulnerabilities. It could guide organizations in allocating security budgets and help researchers reason about when feedback loops actually guarantee protection rather than merely improving it. The analysis distinguishes eventual protection against each fixed attack from complete protection at a single time, and extends to growing attack surfaces, repairs that generalize across related attacks, and multiple discovery mechanisms. Numerical experiments show that faster repair can reduce compromise duration without reducing compromise probability, and the equilibrium regimes include funding neither capability, one, or both.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 9, 04:00

**Background**: Adversarial machine learning studies attacks on ML models and defenses against them, while AI red teaming is a structured adversarial testing process to find flaws before attackers do. The Stackelberg game is a strategic model where a leader (here, the defender) commits to a strategy first and a follower (the attacker) responds optimally. This paper combines these concepts to analyze feedback-driven security investments.

## [Explainable Header-Centric Framework for Semantic Table Interpretation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.10541) ⭐️ 6.0/10

A new arXiv preprint (2610.10541) introduces an explainable, header-centric framework for metadata-only Column Type Annotation (CTA) and Data Quality Assessment (DQA). It maps column headers to 39 interpretable FinalFormat types using curated lexical resources, preserves token-level traceability via SourceKeywords, and aggregates detections into HeadersIQ, a lightweight data source-level quality metric. The framework was evaluated on roughly 120,000 header columns across benchmarks including UCI, Prague, Kaggle, VizNet/Sato, SOTAB, T2Dv2, and the SemTab 2024 Metadata-to-KG track. Metadata-only semantic table interpretation is a critical but under-addressed step in knowledge graph construction, where noisy or missing cell values often make value-based annotation infeasible. By providing an explainable, traceable workflow for header-driven annotation and data quality monitoring, this framework could help data engineers and KG builders prepare cleaner, more trustworthy tabular data before integration. The framework assigns each header a FinalFormat type that activates validation rules from a taxonomy of Data Quality Issues (DQIs), detecting missing data, duplicates, domain violations, wrong data type, and temporal mismatch. On the SemTab 2024 Metadata-to-KG track, official GT-strict evaluation was modest, but a blinded diagnostic audit suggests many mismatches stem from benchmark granularity, aliasing, and ontology-selection effects rather than implausible header-centric predictions; the authors present this audit as diagnostic evidence, not revised benchmark performance.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 9, 04:00

**Background**: Semantic Table Interpretation (STI) is the task of annotating tabular data with semantic types and entities from background knowledge graphs such as DBpedia and Schema.org, and Column Type Annotation (CTA) is a core subtask that assigns semantic labels like 'Person' or 'Location' to columns. Traditional CTA methods rely on cell values, which are often unavailable, noisy, or unsuitable in real-world metadata scenarios. Data Quality Assessment (DQA) is a systematic methodology for determining whether data meets requirements for its intended use, and this paper combines both tasks in a metadata-only, header-centric setting.

## [Confining LLM Agent Self-Evolution to the Runtime Harness with a Hash-Chained Admission Gate](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.10629) ⭐️ 6.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2610.10629) proposes that self-improving LLM agents in credit pipelines should be allowed to evolve only the runtime harness—instruction text, tool-call logic, and primitive composition—while model weights stay fixed, so every adaptation is a reviewable diff with a cause and a test. Evaluated on pre-shift labels the gate rejected every candidate, parametric and scope shifts were repaired locally while a structural shift required primitive replacement, and at the highest structural severity the gate's fixed tolerance blocked the correct replacement in half the seeds.
