This work matters because it draws a sharp, executable line between prediction accuracy, semantic support, and scientific acceptance in representation learning, warning that low prediction error alone cannot justify interpreting latent directions as specific interventions. It is directly relevant to researchers building predictive world models and to safety-critical domains such as vascular device-vessel interaction, where misreading a latent direction as a named intervention could lead to unsupported conclusions. The audit ran 256 additional fits in dimensions 3–24 with prediction equivalence persisting within 4.0e-15, and evaluated nine deliberate runnable fault classes across 64 seeds: all 576 faulty executions completed but each violated at least one reconstruction, prediction, delivered-edit, or scope contract, while all 320 valid control records passed. Repeating a faulty implementation gave exact self-agreement despite error against a separately computed simulator expectation, and scalar-noise experiments exposed both missed weak faults and excessive rejection under narrow relative tolerances.

A new arXiv study evaluated eight newer large language models on the SESR-Eval software engineering systematic review screening benchmark, finding that average Matthews correlation coefficient (MCC) across secondary studies rose only from 0.347 to 0.365 compared to seven older models. A new arXiv paper (2610.10642v1) introduces a discriminative reformulation of the supervised distance for weighted naive Bayes classifiers based on log-odds, and proves that this representation induces a distance that exactly coincides with the L1 distance between vectors of analytical Shapley values. The work also empirically compares several supervised distances derived from these representations using a k-nearest neighbors classifier. This provides a formal explanatory interpretation of the geometry induced by weighted naive Bayes classifiers, bridging supervised distance, local explanation, and predictive behavior. It could help interpretable machine learning researchers better understand how model geometry relates to Shapley-based explanations, though the impact is primarily methodological. The paper starts from the classical supervised distance based on conditional log-likelihoods and introduces a discriminative reformulation based on log-odds, which is more directly related to the classification decision. The empirical comparison uses a k-nearest neighbors classifier, and the work is presented from a primarily methodological perspective with no immediate practical deployment claimed.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 9, 04:00

**Background**: Shapley values, originally from cooperative game theory, are widely used in machine learning to attribute a model's prediction to its input features, and they satisfy desirable axioms such as efficiency. Naive Bayes classifiers are simple probabilistic models that assume conditional independence of features, and weighted variants adjust feature contributions to improve performance. Log-odds (the logit function) expresses the logarithm of the ratio between the probability of an event and its complement, and is commonly used in logistic regression because it is linear in the model parameters. This paper connects these concepts by showing that a particular supervised distance for weighted naive Bayes equals the L1 distance between analytical Shapley values.

## [Epistemic Disturbance in the Graph Model for Conflict Resolution](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.11690) ⭐️ 6.0/10

The paper augments the graph model for conflict resolution (GMCR) by adding decision makers' epistemic states, formally distinguishing state-preserving actions such as announcements, exercises, leaks, and selective disclosures from physical moves and inaction. It builds on a four-valued extension of GMCR that separates evidence for and against a move, showing that evidence for can only enable perceived moves while evidence against can only disable them, and that contradictory assessments are absorbing under monotone accumulation. This provides a formal way to model how actions that leave the physical state unchanged—like leaks or announcements—can shift what other decision makers believe about available moves and intentions, which is central to understanding provocation, deterrence, and strategic signaling in conflicts. It also clarifies which stability concepts are affected by capability versus intention assessments, refining the analytical toolkit for applied conflict analysis. The paper shows that capability assessments affect all sanction-based stability concepts and, on the decision maker's own side, also Nash stability, whereas intention assessments affect only sequential stability. It also demonstrates that in the 1995 DVD format negotiation, general metarationality cannot distinguish its phases because the computer industry group could always sanction, while sequential stability—which asks whether it would—can.

It is relevant to researchers and engineers working on AI accelerators, approximate computing, and medical image segmentation, though as a specialized arXiv preprint it is an incremental rather than immediately industry-disruptive advance. The processing element is synthesized in 45 nm, runs at 500 MHz, occupies 0.858 mm², and consumes 0.726 mJ per 192×192 patch under switching-activity-annotated power analysis; a projected eight-output accelerator with shared activation delivery achieves 16.6 ms latency and 1.67 mJ per patch. Researchers propose the Multi-Perspective Graph Explainer (MPGE), a framework that explains frozen GNN molecular classifiers from three complementary angles: factual support (compact retained edge sets preserving the label), counterfactual sensitivity (bounded deletions that flip the prediction), and exemplar tolerance (non-trivial deletions that preserve the label and confidence). By unifying factual, counterfactual, and exemplar views under one constrained formulation, MPGE addresses a real gap in GNN interpretability and could help chemists and model developers audit molecular classifiers more rigorously. MPGE extends CF-GNNExplainer to graph classification by learning symmetric edge rankings and verifying discrete candidates while recording unsuccessful searches, and a separate BBBP fragment backend returns RDKit-sanitized molecules. ## [BEAT: Adaptive Gradient Modulation Balances Frequency Components for Time-Series Forecasting](https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.19065) ⭐️ 6.0/10

Researchers propose BEAT (Balanced frEquency Adaptive Tuning), a framework that combines a Frequency-Specific Monitor with a Dynamical Gradient Balancer to adjust training emphasis across frequency components for long-term time-series forecasting. Experiments on seven real-world datasets show BEAT achieves competitive performance against state-of-the-art forecasting methods. Frequency-domain methods are a leading paradigm for long-term time-series forecasting, but they lack an explicit mechanism to balance training across frequency components. BEAT's error-dependent gradient weighting offers a general, training-only technique that could be plugged into existing frequency-based forecasters for applications like weather prediction and electricity demand planning. The Frequency-Specific Monitor compares predicted and target wavelet coefficients in a normalized space, expressing each discrepancy relative to a reference error from the detail components; the Dynamical Gradient Balancer converts these ratios into positive, bounded coefficients so higher-error components get larger gradient weights. A shared modulation-strength parameter controls departure from unmodulated training, and both monitoring and balancing are used only during training.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 9, 04:00

**Background**: Long-term time-series forecasting predicts values far into the future and underpins tasks such as weather prediction and electricity demand planning. Frequency-domain methods decompose a series into components at different temporal scales—often via wavelet or Fourier transforms—and model each separately, but a shared forecasting objective does not by itself ensure that each frequency-specific sub-network is trained equally well. Adaptive gradient modulation is a technique that rescales gradients during training to influence how much each part of a model learns.

## [FactorizedHMR: Hybrid Deterministic-Probabilistic Video Human Mesh Recovery](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.14854) ⭐️ 6.0/10

FactorizedHMR introduces a two-stage framework for video human mesh recovery that first recovers a stable torso-root anchor via deterministic regression, then completes ambiguous non-torso articulation using probabilistic flow-matching. It also introduces a synthetic data pipeline providing paired image-camera-motion supervision under diverse viewpoints, and reports the clearest gains in occlusion-heavy recovery and drift-sensitive world-space metrics. Human mesh recovery is fundamentally ambiguous under occlusion or weak depth cues, and treating well-constrained torso/root structure differently from uncertain distal limbs could improve robustness for AR/VR, motion capture, and human-centric video analysis. The hybrid design also shows how probabilistic generative modeling can be combined with deterministic regression in a single pipeline. The method combines a composite target representation, geometry-aware supervision, and feature-aware classifier-free guidance to preserve the torso-root anchor while improving single-reference recovery of ambiguity-prone articulation. It remains competitive with strong baselines across camera-space and world-space benchmarks, with the main caveat that the abstract does not report absolute numbers or comparisons against all state-of-the-art methods.

## [ROAR: Opportunity-Aware Retrieval Refinement for Zero-Shot Time Series Forecasting](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.24911) ⭐️ 6.0/10

ROAR introduces a retrieval opportunity-aware refinement framework for zero-shot time series forecasting that weights training queries by base-forecast difficulty and the relative improvement offered by retrieved candidates, using a learned gate to control correction strength against a fixed base forecaster. Experiments on seven benchmarks show ROAR achieves the lowest average MSE among compared methods, with gains across multiple backbone families and retrieval-augmented forecasters. Retrieval augmentation is increasingly used to give time series foundation models historical continuations, but retrieved candidates that beat the base forecast do not always improve the final prediction. ROAR's opportunity-aware training objective and learned gate offer a principled way to exploit only the useful retrieval opportunities, which could improve zero-shot forecasting reliability for foundation models without in-domain fine-tuning. ROAR first learns to aggregate aligned historical candidates and uses a learned gate to control their correction strength against a fixed base forecaster, then jointly calibrates the forecasting module and gate while anchoring the combined prediction to the first-stage refined output. The paper derives exact decompositions of refinement gains and the opportunity-weighted training loss, and characterizes additional gains from joint calibration under a local linearization.

## [Deep Graph Generative Models Evaluated via Network Science and Immunization Utility](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.01015) ⭐️ 6.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2609.01015v2) evaluates deep graph generative models alongside the classic configuration model from a network science perspective, measuring both topological similarity to real-world networks and their usefulness for identifying effective node immunization strategies against epidemic or misinformation spread. It finds that two deep graph generative models produce synthetic networks that closely resemble the structural properties of real networks, enabling them to identify effective immunization strategies. Because real social contact networks cannot be shared due to privacy risks, synthetic networks are a key alternative for developing and testing epidemic mitigation strategies, so demonstrating that deep generative models can support effective immunization planning could make them a practical substitute for sensitive real data. This cross-disciplinary evaluation also gives network scientists and graph-learning researchers a shared benchmark for judging whether generated graphs are useful, not just realistic-looking. The study compares deep graph generative models against the configuration model, which generates random graphs with a fixed degree sequence, and assesses them on two axes: topological similarity to real networks and utility in identifying effective node immunization strategies. The abstract notes that only two of the deep graph generative models tested achieved synthetic networks close enough to real-world structure to identify effective immunization strategies, implying that not all such models perform equally well.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 9, 04:00

**Background**: Traditional network science models such as the Erdős–Rényi model and the configuration model generate random networks that reproduce only a few selected topological properties of real-world networks; for example, Erdős–Rényi graphs have approximately Poisson degree distributions, unlike most real networks. Deep graph generative models instead learn complex structural distributions directly from real data using deep neural networks, often combining graph neural networks with generative architectures such as VAEs. Node immunization is a standard epidemic-control approach in which selected nodes are removed or vaccinated to slow spreading, and its effectiveness depends heavily on the network's structure.

## [Decentralized Learning Scaling: Topology and Data Dilution Coupled](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.05476) ⭐️ 6.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2610.05476v2) studies how increasing the number of clients N in decentralized learning affects information propagation and consensus, testing N∈{10,50,100,200} on CIFAR-10 with a degree-two Ring, a Static Random graph, and Local-First Heuristic Evolution (LFHE). It shows that the Ring's Metropolis spectral gap decays as Θ(N⁻²), causing progressively slower contraction of model disagreement, while holding nominal local dataset size fixed substantially reduces the apparent population penalty. This work challenges the common assumption that adding more clients automatically degrades decentralized learning, showing that the penalty is largely an artifact of how data is allocated rather than population size alone. It matters for practitioners designing large-scale decentralized or federated training systems, because topology choice and data allocation must be co-designed to avoid unnecessary accuracy loss. The Ring topology provides an analytically transparent failure mode with its Θ(N⁻²) spectral gap decay, while Static Random and LFHE remain close to consensus; increasing LFHE's degree threshold further improves accuracy and consensus but at substantially higher model-transmission cost. The study is limited to CIFAR-10 and specific graph families, so generalization to other datasets and real-world network conditions remains to be validated.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 9, 04:00

**Background**: Decentralized learning trains a shared model across many clients that communicate only with neighbors in a graph, without a central server, using gossip-style averaging. The mixing properties of that graph — often summarized by the spectral gap of the Metropolis weight matrix — determine how quickly clients' models converge to consensus. LFHE is a locally adaptive rewiring process in which each client discovers candidate peers via friend-of-a-friend (FoF) information and tests local edge additions or swaps.

## [GenST Uses LLMs to Forecast Unobserved Sensor Nodes](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.08818) ⭐️ 6.0/10

The paper proposes GenST, a framework that redefines Forecast Unobserved Node States (FUNS) as a conditional generation task on spatio-temporal graphs, using a fine-tuned LLM to extract semantic features from node descriptions such as functional zones and road network structures. It combines a Spatio-Temporal VAE with a Generative Transformer (GenT) that reconstructs future states of unobserved nodes from noise, guided by semantics, geographic coordinates, and neighborhood contexts. Sensor networks often lack comprehensive spatial coverage due to deployment and maintenance costs, so forecasting states of nodes with no historical records is a critical challenge for logistics, urban planning, and intelligent transportation. GenST shows that LLM-derived semantics can compensate for missing spatio-temporal signals, potentially mitigating data sparsity in real-world sensor deployments. The architecture is two-stage: a Spatio-Temporal VAE first compresses spatio-temporal dynamics into a latent space, then a Generative Transformer reconstructs future states from noise under multi-modal conditions. Experiments on six traffic and two non-traffic datasets show GenST significantly outperforms existing baselines in zero-shot prediction tasks.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 9, 04:00

**Background**: Spatio-temporal graph neural networks integrate dynamic graph structures with temporal evolution to predict future signals, and are widely used in urban computing and transportation. FUNS (Forecasting Unobserved Node States) differs from traditional data imputation because it requires inductive generalization: learning universal spatio-temporal patterns from observed nodes and transferring them to unseen nodes in a zero-shot manner. Variational autoencoders (VAEs) are deep latent variable models that enable fast, scalable inference on large, structured datasets, making them suitable for compressing complex spatio-temporal dynamics.

## [Gated Cross Attention Framework Detects Emotionally Rewritten Fake News](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.08835) ⭐️ 6.0/10

This paper investigates fake news detection under fact-preserving emotional variations and proposes a Gated Cross Attention (GCA) framework that adaptively integrates emotionally rewritten news with LLM-generated explanations from the original articles. Experiments on PolitiFact, GossipCop, and LUN show notable improvements under multiple emotional conditions on PolitiFact and LUN, while maintaining competitive performance on GossipCop. This work addresses a realistic and understudied vulnerability in fake news detection: emotional reframing that preserves factual claims can degrade model robustness, and the proposed use of stable LLM-generated explanations as background knowledge offers a practical way to mitigate this. It has implications for NLP researchers and platforms building misinformation detection systems that must remain reliable across varied emotional presentations. The GCA framework uses gating mechanisms to focus on informative explanation content while reducing mismatches caused by emotional reframing, and the authors provide code and data at a GitHub repository. The paper also analyzes the effects of explanation guidance and gating mechanisms under different emotional conditions.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 9, 04:00

**Background**: Fake news detection methods often rely on stylistic cues or external information, but news articles are frequently rewritten with different emotional tones while keeping the same factual claims, which can fool detectors. Gated cross-attention is a neural mechanism that uses learned gates to selectively fuse information from different sources, suppressing noise and emphasizing reliable signals. Large language models can generate explanations from original articles that serve as stable background knowledge, helping models stay robust when the surface text changes emotionally.

## [MaRK Dynamically Conditions Frozen SSMs via Markov-Adapted Recurrent Kernels](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09092) ⭐️ 6.0/10

MaRK (Markov-adapted Recurrent Kernels) is a new framework that maps context vectors directly into bounded modulations of a frozen State Space Model's recurrence (A), read-in (B), read-out (C), skip (D), and discretization (Δ) parameters. Instantiated on a frozen 111M-parameter Hydra SSM backbone, it uses Hypernet, Chebyshev polynomial, and DCT adapter geometries, with the Chebyshev variant achieving the best average validation loss of 2.55 using only 6.3–11M trainable auxiliary parameters. This work shows that conditioning pre-trained SSMs can be moved inside the recurrent operator rather than applied only through input injection or activation modulation, potentially enabling more expressive and stable iterative generation such as diffusion. Because parameter-efficient fine-tuning emerges structurally from the low-rank adapters, it offers a practical path to repurpose bidirectional SSM backbones for iterative diffusion regimes without retraining the full model. The bounded recurrence parameterization yields an analytic Affine Quadratic Stability certificate for the modulated recurrence, and synthetic LPV recovery experiments plus Markov-operator diagnostics show MaRK recovers coordinate-invariant temporal operators under matched assumptions. The DCT variant reaches 2.59 and the Hypernet variant 3.77, indicating that adapter geometry materially affects performance.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 9, 04:00

**Background**: State Space Models (SSMs) are a class of sequence models, rooted in control theory, that represent a dynamic system through state variables and offer an efficient alternative to Transformers. Linear Parameter-Varying (LPV) state-space models are systems whose parameters vary with an external scheduling signal, providing a theoretical lens for context-dependent dynamics. Hydra is a modular SSM architecture that combines a Mamba-style state-space backbone with sparse attention, mixture-of-experts, and dual memories for efficient long-context reasoning.
